articles.title: Up to 50% of donated items are unsellable for Jersey charity
articles.summary: Cameron Honey from Acorn Enterprises says damaged and unwashed items take hours to deal with.
articles.body:
A charity shop has said about 30 to 50% of items given to its donation centre are not sellable because they are not in good enough condition.

Acorn Enterprises said items it had donated included unwashed socks and underwear, which then takes time and resources to remove.

Volunteers and staff at the charity's donation centre spend hours sorting through the items.

Cameron Honey from the charity said it was grateful for donations but "it would be nice to see people taking maybe a bit more care in what they donate".

Honey wants more people to be aware of the impact the donations have on charities.

He said: "We do appreciate donations because if we didn't get them then we wouldn't be able to stay afloat.

"But a lot of the stuff doesn't seem to have been washed and it's not nice going through a bag of clothes and finding used socks and used underwear.

"It would be nice to see people take a bit more care in what they donate and think whether they would sell it."

Tess West uses her social media account Tat and Treasures to promote second-hand shopping in Jersey and was given a tour of the donation centre to see the issue.

She said: "I don't understand how some of these things have not been through the wash... people are literally giving dirty clothes and using it as a dump rather than a charity shop."

She added: "I think from my perspective what I see in charity shops in general - there are incredible clothes, especially children's clothes, which are fantastic in charity shops.

"So I think it's just about being conscious when you're donating your items."

West also commented on the impact of the growing number of fast fashion clothes, which are quickly and cheaply produced, ending up in charity shops.

She said: "There is a lot more fast fashion in our charity shops than we have ever seen... let's educate people on not buying those things in the first place."

Honey agreed the items are hard for charities like Acorn to handle: "They're not really sellable because they just don't really last that long at all."

articles.title: Município isolado no Acre enfrenta falta de alimentos devido à seca | G1
articles.standfirst: Comunidades do Jordão têm dificuldade para conseguir mantimentos e gás de cozinha. Cidade é uma das que não possuem ligação terrestre com o restante do estado e depende de transporte fluvial para abastecimento.
articles.summary: Comunidades do Jordão têm dificuldade para conseguir mantimentos e gás de cozinha. Cidade é uma das que não têm ligação terrestre com os demais e depende de transporte fluvial.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A estiagem dos rios Muru e Tarauacá está provocando desabastecimento em comunidade ribeirinhas e indígenas de Jordão, interior do Acre, uma das cidades acreanas que não têm ligação terrestre com as demais.

Devido ao isolamento, o transporte de alimentos e outros produtos depende de embarcações e é prejudicado pela redução no nível dos mananciais da região.

Um morador da comunidade Novo Porto registrou em vídeo o baixo nível das águas do Rio Muru. "A comunidade hoje se encontra sem nenhum mantimento. Não tem como os comerciantes e demais comunitários daqui da comunidade irem buscar seu mantimento nos municípios. Minha gente, aqui não tem gás, não tem nada e está faltando tudo", relata. (Veja acima)

Em vídeo gravado nesta segunda-feira (23), um morador relatou a falta de mantimentos e gás — Foto: Reprodução

Em outro registro, moradores da comunidade Novo Segredo e Bom Futuro alertam para as dificuldades de navegação: "Estamos tentando virar o bote, mas o rio está tão estreito que não quer virar. É a nossa realidade, o rio está cobrindo o pé, o negócio aqui está sério", diz.

Com a repercussão das imagens, o Governo do Acre informou que articula uma ação de assistência humanitária para atender a população afetada pela estiagem no município.

De acordo com a Defesa Civil Estadual, a previsão é que as cestas básicas cheguem ao município ainda nesta semana. A ação é organizada em parceria com a Secretaria de Assistência Social e Direitos Humanos (Seasdh) e a gestão municipal.

Além disso, o prefeito de Jordão, Naudo Ribeiro (PP), afirmou ao g1 que as equipes estão sendo mobilizadas para prestar assistência às famílias atingidas pela estiagem. Segundo ele, o município também está na fase final de aquisição de cestas básicas.

Seca nos rios Muru e Tarauacá isolou a comunidade Novo Porto, Novo Segredo e Bom Futuro no Jordão — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

O gestor explicou que a definição dos locais prioritários depende de um levantamento sobre as comunidades mais prejudicadas. Ele destacou ainda que o transporte da ajuda humanitária é um dos principais desafios, principalmente nas localidades mais distantes.

"Para levar assistência para esses locais, essas aldeias, as comunidades mais afastadas dos municípios, é uma dificuldade bem maior. Muitas vezes só a aeronave consegue chegar, ou então pequenas embarcações que levam pouca quantidade de assistência", afirmou.

O prefeito disse ainda, que o município acompanha a situação em conjunto com órgãos estaduais e instituições responsáveis pelo atendimento às populações indígenas e ribeirinhas, além da Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai).

A dificuldade de acesso e os impactos da estiagem não são novos para os moradores de Jordão. Em setembro de 2025, o município teve autorizado um repasse de R$ 331.522,80 do Ministério da Integração e do Desenvolvimento Regional (MIDR) para ações emergenciais da Defesa Civil.

À época, os recursos foram destinados a medidas de resposta e recuperação diante dos efeitos de desastres naturais. Entre as ações previstas estavam a distribuição de cestas básicas, kits de higiene e água potável, além de outras medidas de assistência à população afetada.

A estiagem atual volta a evidenciar a dependência das comunidades rurais e ribeirinhas do transporte fluvial e os desafios para garantir o abastecimento em períodos de redução do nível dos rios.

articles.title: VÍDEO: Caminhão afunda em aterro ao tentar atravessar ponte no RS | G1
articles.standfirst: Motorista conseguiu sair do veículo sem ferimentos. Caso aconteceu nesta terça-feira, em Ibirubá, na Região Noroeste do estado.
articles.summary: Motorista conseguiu sair do veículo sem ferimentos. Caso aconteceu nesta terça-feira, em Ibirubá, na Região Noroeste do estado.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Um temporal causou estragos no município de Ibirubá , na Região Noroeste do Rio Grande do Sul, nesta terça-feira (24). A precipitação provocou a queda de um caminhão em uma travessia, destelhou casas e derrubou árvores na cidade.

O acidente com o veículo de carga ocorreu na localidade de Rincão Seco , na zona rural do município. Conforme a Defesa Civil, a ponte da região estava bloqueada havia mais de um mês . Para permitir o trânsito, um aterro provisório funcionava no local.

Devido ao volume de água acumulado e ao peso do transporte, a estrutura improvisada cedeu e o caminhão caiu . O condutor conseguiu abandonar a cabine e escapou sem ferimentos .

Por conta do bloqueio na via, os moradores de Rincão Seco ficaram sem ligação direta com a área urbana de Ibirubá. Temporariamente, a única rota de saída da comunidade é seguir em direção ao município de Cruz Alta.

Em publicação nas redes sociais, a prefeitura de Ibirubá informou que "o prefeito em exercício, Tuta Rebelato, esteve percorrendo localidades de Ibirubá, verificando os estragos causados pelas fortes chuvas e acompanhando os trabalhos realizados pelas equipes da Secretaria de Obras. A Administração Municipal segue mobilizada para recuperar os locais atingidos".

Até a metade da manhã desta terça-feira, o índice pluviométrico na cidade atingiu 87 milímetros. O mau tempo também arrancou os telhados de aproximadamente 10 residências e provocou a queda de vegetação em diversos pontos do município.

🚫 A orientação é evitar áreas inundáveis e permanecer em local seguro. Em caso de emergência, os moradores devem acionar a Brigada Militar pelo telefone 190 ou o Corpo de Bombeiros pelo 193. Segundo a Defesa Civil, eletroeletrônicos devem ser retirados da tomada durante os temporais. Portas e janelas precisam permanecer fechadas, e os animais domésticos devem ser abrigados.

⚠️ Em caso de enxurrada, a orientação é colocar documentos e objetos de valor em sacos plásticos. Se a situação de grande perigo for confirmada, os moradores devem procurar abrigo e evitar permanecer ao ar livre.

articles.title: Senior Hamas security official killed in Israeli drone strikes
articles.summary: A senior Hamas security official has been killed in a series of Israeli strikes across Gaza
articles.body:
Senior Hamas security official killed in Israeli drone strikes

A senior Hamas security official has been killed in a series of Israeli strikes across Gaza, which also killed three police officers and three brothers, including a child. Medical teams are struggling to treat dozens of injured people amid restrictions on medical supplies and medication. Hind Khoudary reports from Gaza City.

articles.title: Bombeiros são condenados no Chile por incêndio com 138 mortos | G1
articles.standfirst: Em fevereiro de 2024, vários incêndios florestais começaram simultaneamente em Viña del Mar, cidade a 110 km de Santiago. O calor e as fortes rajadas de vento, em pleno verão, espalharam rapidamente as chamas.
articles.summary: Em fevereiro de 2024, vários incêndios florestais começaram simultaneamente em Viña del Mar, cidade a 110 km de Santiago.
articles.body:
Foto de 4 de fevereiro de 2024 mostra carros destruídos em rua de Viña del Mar após incêndios florestais no Chile — Foto: Sofia Yanjari/Reuters

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Um tribunal do Chile condenou nesta terça-feira (24) sete bombeiros e brigadistas florestais por provocarem os incêndios que devastaram a cidade litorânea de Viña del Mar, em fevereiro de 2024, e deixaram 138 mortos , informou o Ministério Público do país.

Em 2 de fevereiro daquele ano, vários incêndios florestais começaram simultaneamente nos arredores da cidade, 110 km a noroeste de Santiago. O calor e as fortes rajadas de vento, em pleno verão no Hemisfério Sul, espalharam rapidamente as chamas.

As investigações do Ministério Público concluíram que os incêndios foram provocados intencionalmente por bombeiros e brigadistas florestais para aumentar a remuneração com horas extras.

Sete dos nove acusados "foram condenados como autores de um crime de incêndio com resultado de morte", informou o Ministério Público em um comunicado.

O órgão informou à AFP que pediu prisão perpétua para os condenados . As penas serão anunciadas em audiência prevista para 18 de dezembro. Eles também foram condenados por crimes de incêndio florestal e associação criminosa.

O incêndio florestal de Viña del Mar foi o segundo mais mortífero do mundo neste século , depois do devastador incêndio registrado em 2009 no sudeste da Austrália, que causou a morte de pelo menos 173 pessoas.

articles.title: Pátio de veículos de Piracicaba terá concessão de 25 anos; entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Medida prevê que empresa interessada tenha área de 15 mil m² para abrigar 1,25 mil carros e motos, serviço de guincho e apoio aos leilões. Prefeitura alega economia com frota e infraestrutura.
articles.summary: Medida prevê que empresa interessada tenha área de 15 mil m² para abrigar 1,25 mil carros e motos, serviço de guincho e apoio aos leilões. Prefeitura alega economia.
articles.body:
Remoção de veículo em Piracicaba — Foto: Isabela Borghese/ Prefeitura de Piracicaba

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A Prefeitura de Piracicaba (SP) publicou no Diário Oficial, de quinta-feira (19), um ato que justifica a concessão do pátio municipal de veículos à iniciativa privada por 25 anos.

O contrato de concessão está estimado em R$ 72,9 milhões para os 300 meses, e a empresa vencedora será escolhida por concorrência eletrônica e vencerá a que apresentar a maior oferta de pagamento inicial (outorga inicial). Segundo a administração municipal, o modelo foi adotado para reduzir gastos públicos e transferir à concessionária os custos da operação.

A transferência do serviço de remoção, depósito e guarda de veículos apreendidos por infrações de trânsito para a iniciativa privada foi autorizada em novembro de 2025, por meio da Lei Municipal 10.459.

A publicação da Secretaria Municipal de Segurança Pública, Trânsito e Transportes é uma etapa obrigatória antes da abertura oficial da licitação.

O valor mínimo estimado para o contrato é de R$ 72,9 milhões ao longo de 25 anos, cerca de R$ 2,9 milhões por ano;

A empresa vencedora deverá oferecer um pátio com área mínima de 15 mil m²;

O espaço deverá comportar cerca de 1.250 veículos;

A concessionária ficará responsável por serviços como guincho, remoção, guarda, liberação de veículos e apoio aos leilões;

Veículos em pátio de Piracicaba — Foto: Reprodução/Eptv

A empresa vencedora será responsável por toda a estrutura do pátio. Isso inclui guinchos, equipes de atendimento, sistemas de informação, seguros e segurança patrimonial permanente.

O contrato prevê o recolhimento de carros e motos apreendidos, retidos, acidentados ou abandonados em vias públicas de Piracicaba. O serviço deverá seguir as regras do Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB).

A concessionária será paga por meio das tarifas cobradas diretamente dos donos dos veículos pelos serviços de remoção e permanência no pátio.

Em troca do direito de explorar o serviço, a empresa terá de pagar ao município um valor fixo na assinatura do contrato. Também deverá repassar 5% do faturamento bruto mensal.

A prefeitura diz que escolheu o modelo de concessão por razões técnicas e para economizar recursos públicos.

Segundo o documento assinado pelo secretário municipal de Segurança Pública, Trânsito e Transportes, Odair Luiz de Melo, a operação direta do serviço exigiria investimentos da prefeitura. Entre eles estão gastos com terreno, frota própria de guinchos e pessoal.

Nesse modelo, a empresa assume os custos e os riscos financeiros da operação. Já o poder público continua responsável pela regulamentação do serviço, pela fiscalização do trânsito e pela aplicação de penalidades.

A escolha da futura concessionária será feita por concorrência eletrônica, em disputa aberta. Vencerá a empresa habilitada que oferecer o maior valor inicial à prefeitura. Os prazos para envio das propostas serão informados quando a prefeitura publicar o edital.

articles.title: Chinesa Huawei é condenada nos EUA por negócios no Irã e roubo de segredos comerciais; entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Processo criminal começou em 2018, quando autoridades americanas intensificaram investigações sobre a empresa. Julgamento durou mais de dois meses.
articles.summary: Processo criminal começou em 2018, quando autoridades americanas intensificaram investigações sobre a empresa. Julgamento durou mais de dois meses.
articles.body:
Chinesa Huawei é condenada nos EUA — Foto: Hannibal Hanschke/Reuters

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A chinesa Huawei foi condenada nesta terça-feira (24) em um amplo processo criminal nos Estados Unidos. A gigante de tecnologia e equipamentos de telecomunicações foi acusada de enganar bancos sobre seus negócios no Irã e roubar segredos comerciais de empresas americanas.

Um júri federal do Brooklyn considerou a Huawei culpada de 10 das 12 acusações criminais que enfrentava. A empresa foi absolvida da acusação de conspiração para a prática de atividades criminosas organizadas, baseada na alegação de que atuava como uma organização criminosa.

Em comunicado, a Huawei afirmou que as acusações pelas quais foi condenada não têm fundamento jurídico e que tomará "todas as medidas legais necessárias para defender nossos direitos e interesses".

As autoridades americanas tinham a Huawei na mira havia anos, sob o argumento de que a empresa representava riscos à segurança nacional. O processo criminal começou em 2018 e, no ano seguinte, o governo dos EUA incluiu a companhia chinesa em uma lista de restrições comerciais, limitando seu acesso à tecnologia americana.

Especialistas afirmam, no entanto, que o caso não prejudicou os negócios da Huawei. Isso porque a empresa diversificou suas atividades e se tornou uma das principais companhias chinesas no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial.

O julgamento durou mais de dois meses. A acusação convocou mais de 60 testemunhas, enquanto a defesa apresentou 15.

A Huawei e três empresas afiliadas enfrentavam 12 acusações, incluindo conspiração para a prática de atividades criminosas organizadas, fraude bancária, fraude eletrônica, violações de sanções e conspiração para roubar segredos comerciais e obstruir a Justiça.

"Depois que a imprensa começou a questionar as operações da Huawei no Irã, os bancos que trabalhavam com a empresa também passaram a fazer perguntas", afirmou a promotora Meredith Arfa aos jurados durante suas alegações finais.

Filha do fundador da empresa chegou a ser detida

O caso ganhou destaque em dezembro de 2018, quando Meng Wanzhou, diretora financeira da Huawei e filha do fundador da companhia, foi detida no Canadá com base em um mandado de prisão americano. A detenção provocou uma crise diplomática envolvendo EUA, China e Canadá.

Meng havia sido acusada formalmente, sob sigilo, de supostamente enganar um funcionário do banco HSBC sobre os negócios da Huawei no Irã, permitindo que a empresa movimentasse dólares para dentro e para fora do país em violação às sanções americanas.

Ela contestou sua extradição para os Estados Unidos durante quase três anos, até firmar um acordo que suspendeu o processo criminal sob determinadas condições e retornar à China, onde foi recebida como heroína.

As acusações contra ela foram retiradas.

Promotores acusaram empresa de roubar segredos comerciais

A acusação formal apresentada em 2018 sustentava que a Huawei havia enganado os bancos HSBC, Standard Chartered e BNP Paribas sobre suas relações comerciais com o Irã.

Em 2020, os promotores acrescentaram novas acusações, incluindo a de que a Huawei havia conspirado para roubar segredos comerciais de empresas americanas de tecnologia ao longo de duas décadas.

Durante o julgamento, os promotores tentaram demonstrar que a Huawei:

Roubou códigos-fonte da Cisco Systems utilizados em seus roteadores;

Apropriou-se de tecnologia de antenas da empresa de telecomunicações sem fio Quintel;

Contratou um professor para obter acesso a uma placa de circuito desenvolvida pela fabricante de semicondutores CNEX.

Os jurados assistiram a um vídeo que, segundo os promotores, mostrava um funcionário da Huawei colocando discretamente na mochila uma peça de um robô de testes da T-Mobile.

Eles também ouviram relatos sobre um engenheiro da Huawei que teria entrado discretamente no estande da Fujitsu durante uma feira comercial para fotografar um equipamento.

Os promotores apresentaram aos jurados uma declaração anexada ao acordo de suspensão do processo criminal firmado por Meng, na qual ela reconheceu que a empresa havia realizado negócios ilegais no Irã.

Meng não testemunhou durante o julgamento, mas um funcionário do HSBC com quem ela se reuniu em 2013 prestou depoimento.

Defesa afirma que bancos sabiam dos negócios com o Irã

A defesa argumentou que o HSBC e os demais bancos tinham conhecimento dos negócios da Huawei no Irã e disputavam a oportunidade de prestar serviços à companhia.

Brian Heberlig, advogado da Huawei, acusou os promotores, durante suas alegações finais, de terem "selecionado a dedo" alguns episódios isolados para sustentar a acusação de uma conspiração que teria durado 20 anos.

Segundo ele, a Huawei alcançou o sucesso por meio de "trabalho árduo, inovação e investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento".

A empresa tem mais de 200 mil funcionários e opera em aproximadamente 170 países.

articles.title: Moradores esperam há 8 anos por solução após interdição de casas | G1
articles.standfirst: Famílias deixaram os imóveis em 2018 após rachaduras e afundamentos em São Carlos (SP); algumas vivem com aluguel social de R$ 700 e aguardam definição sobre indenizações.
articles.summary: Famílias deixaram os imóveis em 2018 após rachaduras e afundamentos em São Carlos (SP); algumas vivem com aluguel social de R$ 700 e aguardam definição sobre indenizações.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O que era para ser uma medida de segurança se transformou em uma longa espera por respostas. Moradores retirados de casas no Jardim Gonzaga, em São Carlos (SP), devido ao risco de desabamento, cobram uma solução da prefeitura quase 8 anos após a interdição dos imóveis.

Em nota, a Prefeitura de São Carlos disse que acompanha o problema com as casas desde 2018, quando uma avaliação técnica identificou ampliações dos imóveis, como construção de pavimentos perto do muro de arrimo, sem acompanhamento técnico, o que pode ter motivado a instabilidade e colapso do terreno, e que foi necessário demolir alguns imóveis para construir um novo muro de arrimo. (Veja o restante do posicionamento abaixo).

As famílias foram obrigadas a deixar as residências em 2018 após rachaduras e afundamentos que passaram a comprometer a estrutura das construções. Desde então, algumas recebem aluguel social de R$ 700. Uma promessa de indenização, segundo os moradores, não foi cumprida.

Quase 8 anos após interdição de casas, moradores ainda esperam indenização em São Carlos, SP — Foto: EPTV/Reprodução

A lavadora de carros Maira Nunes Fernandes viveu por 6 anos em uma casa da Rua Aparecida Basílio de Camargo Silva. Ela contou que precisou deixar o imóvel quando parte das construções da área começou a apresentar risco de desabamento.

"São cinco famílias sem casa, pagando aluguel e [que] não podem ter suas residências para morar com criança", afirmou Maira.

Segundo os moradores, os problemas começaram após a construção de um muro nos fundos dos terrenos , separando as casas de um campo de futebol do projeto Cemear, que oferece atividades no contraturno escolar para crianças e adolescentes.

Moradores relatam que problema aconteceu após construção de muro no fundo das residências em São Carlos, SP — Foto: EPTV/Reprodução

De acordo com a lavadora de carros, laudos e perícias apontaram a presença de uma mina d'água no local. "Mesmo assim, a prefeitura ergueu o muro em cima da mina. E a mina começou a jorrar água para dentro das casas e foi onde começou as rachaduras."

A dona de casa Maria Aparecida enfrenta situação semelhante. Retirada do imóvel em 2018, ela viu a casa ser demolida quatro anos depois. Segundo ela, o aluguel social recebido atualmente, de R$ 700, não é suficiente para cobrir os custos de uma moradia.

"Fui morar de aluguel social, só que esses R$ 700 que eles dão não é o suficiente para a gente pagar um casa. O dono da casa quer aumento agora e eu não tenho como aumentar", disse.

Quase 8 anos após interdição de casas, moradores ainda esperam indenização em São Carlos — Foto: EPTV/Reprodução

Os moradores contaram que compraram as casas, possuem escritura e que sempre pagaram impostos, ou seja, tudo estava regular quando os terrenos começaram a ceder. "A casa foi trincando, foi abrindo tudo, tudo. O chão começou a abaixar e começou aquela bagunça, né?", afirmou Maria.

Além das três casas que foram demolidas, outras três residências permanecem interditadas pela Defesa Civil Municipal. Em algumas delas, as rachaduras são visíveis e parte do piso apresenta sinais de afundamento.

A auxiliar de limpeza Sheila Aparecida Barroso morou por três anos em uma das casas interditadas. Ela deixou o imóvel por questões de segurança e passou a pagar aluguel. "Está perigoso, né? Em qualquer momento pode cair."

Chão de uma das casas interditadas, em São Carlos, está afundando — Foto: EPTV/Reprodução

Sheila afirmou que, quase 8 anos após ter deixado o imóvel e alugar outra casa, ainda não recebeu nenhum aluguel social e que o problema só aumenta.

"Querendo ou não, a gente está pagando aluguel e a gente não tem um dinheiro para a gente ficar pagando aluguel direto, né? E é ruim. Assim, eles não falam nada, não resolvem nada e fica difícil", complementou.

Para Maira, a situação se tornou insustentável. "Eu quero uma resposta porque eu não posso nem construir, nem morar. E R$ 700 de aluguel com 4 crianças, o que eu faço? Sendo que o meu aluguel é R$ 1,2 mil."

A dona de casa teme não conseguir manter a moradia atual. "Eu não tenho aonde entrar. Se eu sair aquela casa, eu tenho que morar na rua. É na rua que eu tenho que morar. Eu não tenho dinheiro para pagar aluguel."

A administração municipal informou que desde fevereiro de 2020 concede aluguel social para as famílias, mas não disse se o valor será reajustado.

A prefeitura disse, também, que a Secretaria Municipal de Desenvolvimento Urbano abriu processo administrativo para avaliar se existe direito à indenização para as famílias que perderam as casas.

articles.title: Chuva em Indaiatuba provoca alagamentos e queda de árvores | G1
articles.standfirst: Temporal desta terça-feira (24) ainda provocou a suspensão de aulas na Fiec; apesar dos estragos, não houve registro de vítimas e desabrigados.
articles.summary: Com 40,9 mm de chuva em uma hora, Indaiatuba registra quedas de árvores e alagamentos que levaram à suspensão das aulas na Fiec; não há registro de vítimas na cidade.
articles.body:
Morador registrou alagamento na Av. Eng. Fábio Roberto Barnabé, em Indaiatuba (SP), nesta terça-feira (24) — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A forte chuva que atingiu Indaiatuba (SP) no fim da tarde desta terça-feira (24) provocou alagamentos, quedas de árvores, interdição de rua e a suspensão de aulas na Fundação Indaiatubana de Educação e Cultura (Fiec). Segundo a prefeitura, foram registrados 40,9 milímetros de precipitação em uma hora .

Não havia registro de vítimas nem de pessoas desabrigadas até a última atualização desta reportagem.

De acordo com a administração, a intensidade da chuva causou pontos isolados de alagamento em diferentes regiões da cidade, mas que já foram normalizadas. Até as 17h30, o município contabilizava oito quedas de árvores .

Equipes da prefeitura foram mobilizadas para atuar no corte e remoção dos exemplares, além da limpeza e desobstrução das áreas atingidas.

A Rua Eurico Primo Venturine permanece interditada . Também foi registrado o desabamento de parte do muro de um condomínio .

Por causa dos danos causados pela chuva, as aulas da Fiec foram suspensas na noite desta terça-feira e também na manhã de quarta-feira (25). A expectativa é de que as atividades sejam retomadas no período da tarde.

"A administração municipal orienta que a população evite áreas alagadas, não tente atravessar trechos com grande volume de água e procure locais seguros durante ocorrências de chuva intensa", destacou, em nota.

Em Campinas, a chuva provocou quatro ocorrências sem registro de vítimas nesta terça-feira (24).

Segundo a Defesa Civil, houve duas quedas de árvores, uma na Rua Loja Maçônica Independência, no Residencial Novo Mundo, e outra na Rua Professor Otílio Guernelli, no Jardim Lisa, além de um destelhamento e uma queda de muro na Rua Hilário Baldo, no Conjunto Mauro Marcondes.

De acordo com o Cepagri da Unicamp, o município registrou acumulado de 5,8 milímetros de chuva, com ventos de até 39,9 km/h às 17h40.

Já dados da estação meteorológica de Viracopos apontam velocidade máxima do vento de 35,18 km/h às 16h40 e rajada de 68,52 km/h durante o temporal.

articles.title: Rain warning in place across Cornwall and Isles of Scilly
articles.summary: The Met Office issues a yellow rain warning across Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly for Tuesday.
articles.body:
A yellow weather warning for rain is currently in place across Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly.

The Met Office said the warning would be in place from 08:01 GMT on Tuesday until 23:59 and warned heavy rain could cause some flooding and travel disruption.

It said a band of heavy rain would slowly move across the county throughout the day before easing overnight, with about 30mm to 40mm (1.2in to 1.6in) of rain expected to fall.

The persistent rain has caused some roads to flood and Cornwall Council has urged people not to walk or drive through floodwater.

The Environment Agency issued a number of flood alerts , meaning flooding is possible.

Meanwhile, a flood warning has been issued for the River Hayle in Cornwall, meaning flooding is "expected" from Relubbus to St Erth.

River levels are forecast to be at their highest in the area overnight, with residents urged to "act now" and follow official advice.

That includes moving to a safe location and turning off gas and electricity at home if safe to do so.

Dave Clarke, from the Kernow Weather Team, said more than 40mm (1.6in) of rain had already fallen in parts of Cornwall, which had led to flooding and standing water.

He said central to west Cornwall faced "the brunt of the rain with some intense downpours".

The Met Office said there was a chance persistent heavy downpours in some parts of west Cornwall could result in more than 60mm (2.4in) of rainfall.

It warned spray and flooding could lead to difficult driving conditions and some road closures, with delays or cancellations to train and bus services possible.

The Met Office added there was a small chance homes and businesses could be flooded, as well as a low risk of power cuts and loss of other services.

Cornwall Council has urged people to take extra care around beaches and coastal paths, and to stay away from waves breaking over seafronts and coastal defences.

It said a section of the A30 between Trereife crossroads and Mount Misery was closed earlier due to flooding. It has since reopened.

Train services between Liskeard and Looe have been suspended, with heavy rainfall causing flooding along the line in several parts, Great Western Railway said.

articles.title: Chicago's biggest welfare recipients are the politicians at City Hall
articles.summary: Mayor Brandon Johnson's Chicago added $1.9 billion in debt since 2023, while a South Side leader says the real "welfare queens" sit in City Hall.
articles.body: Every now and then, I hear the term "welfare queen." I know what people mean by a phrase popularized in the 1980s. Say "welfare queen," and I know a stereotype pops into your mind — and it isn’t a good one. It is true that some exploit and take advantage of the system to the max. For them, "welfare queen" is apt. In my line of work, however, I’ve sat with single mothers working two or three jobs, stretching their paychecks to the end of the month. Many have set up savings accounts to build the capital needed to make the jump from welfare to the independent life they crave. Nearly all of them were born into this world of dependency, and they are determined to end the intergenerational cycle of cultural dependency. There’s nothing "welfare queen" about them. Just "queen." The biggest welfare recipients in this city are not the mothers in my neighborhood. They are the politicians downtown who have turned Chicago’s roughly $55 billion debt into a career. PASTOR COREY BROOKS: HOW THE WELFARE STATE BROKE THE BLACK FAMILY, AND HOW TO FIX IT Since Mayor Brandon Johnson took office in 2023, he and the city have added another $1.9 billion to their debt obligations. Debt and pension payments already consume billions every year — more than $3.6 billion out of the current budget, with nearly $4 billion projected next year just to stay current. He brags that he has the "Blackest" administration, yet we don’t see the city’s budget going to the Blackest schools, where literacy and math rates are dismal. Our Blackest neighborhoods are riddled with potholes, there’s garbage in the gutters and there are no city-funded pathways to real opportunities. (I’m obviously using "Blackest" facetiously here.) Here’s a quick look at how some of the money is being spent. The administration wants to borrow roughly $481 million to settle police misconduct lawsuits, including a $260.8 million deal tied to former Detective Reynaldo Guevara for 17 men who spent a combined 384 years in prison. In 2026 alone, the city has already paid more than $277 million on these cases. Officials also borrowed $166 million to cover four years of back pay for firefighters because they never set the cash aside when the costs were known. A plan to refinance debt that was supposed to generate $65 million to $71 million produced only about $36 million. A scheme to sell roughly $1 billion in old city-owed debt for nearly $90 million went nowhere — banks walked away. Other hoped-for revenues from ads on light poles and similar ideas never materialized. Now, the city faces an $882 million deficit and still wants more borrowing and higher taxes. CHICAGO MAYOR BRANDON JOHNSON FIGHTS TO STAY ON 2027 BALLOT AMID CITY HALL EXODUS, CREDIT WARNING While they borrow from banks and tax hardworking people, City Hall has protected its own: the government employee. There have been no real layoffs, no furloughs, no pay freezes and no meaningful shared sacrifice for the people who draw city salaries and pensions. Hiring freezes were announced and then quietly ignored. Not only that, hundreds of hires continued, including senior roles in the mayor’s own office. The political class keeps its jobs, comfortable raises and benefits while the debt grows and neighborhoods like mine are left to pay the price. That is not austerity. That is the system taking care of itself first. You would think the "Blackest" administration would care. It recently got worse. The resignation of Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch, the third person to hold that job in a year, makes the picture clearer. She quit after just three months, saying that continuing would compromise her integrity and her obligation to give accurate statements to investors, rating agencies, the City Council and taxpayers. She used the word "integrity" and resigned. CHICAGO PASTOR GATHERS HUNDREDS OF MEN TO DECLARE VIOLENCE-FREE ZONE ON SOUTH SIDE Her crime was doing the right thing by contradicting the claim that the mayor’s budget was mostly structurally balanced. She pointed out that borrowing to cover settlements is not a lasting solution. Now, City Council members are moving to authorize an independent outside review of the city’s financial statements over the past three years. The fact that Gabrysch would rather resign than be compromised reveals the extent of the corruption in Johnson’s administration. The irony for me is that I have raised millions of dollars without government help to build a 90,000-square-foot community center on the South Side designed to educate our youth and provide them with an abundance of opportunities. We have the trades, the church, the mentors, the safety, the tutoring and much more. Most of all, we improved the city without its help. DIVINE PURPOSE HELPED BRING CHICAGO’S MOST-DANGEROUS BLOCK BACK TO LIFE I’m not against help at all. In fact, I would welcome it because I believe a City Hall invested in the real progress of all its people is much needed. What I am against is a political culture that keeps promising that one more tax, one more program or one more bond will finally deliver transformation — all while the numbers on literacy, family structure and economic mobility stay stubbornly bad. That is why I firmly believe in what Alexis de Tocqueville saw in America almost 200 years ago. He saw what made America different and wrote that Americans of all ages and backgrounds will often create associations and volunteer their time to better their part of the world. They create these associations to fix potholes, raise churches, build schools and so on. That is what my neighbors and I did on the South Side. We are living proof that Tocqueville’s observation remains alive today in America. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION It is his warning, however, that we must heed. The more government takes the place of associations, the more individuals lose the idea of forming them. When they lose that idea, they become dependent on the government — and that, in turn, gives the government the license to run up the debt, which is the truth of what has happened to us. That is the vicious cycle we live in, and we must stop it. My example on the South Side of Chicago proves that we can. I continue to eliminate the "welfare queens" in my neighborhood by showing them the way out of a life of dependency. Will we have the courage to show the "welfare queens" in City Hall the way out? articles.title: Sundar Pichai-backed San Francisco-based family foundation recorded $9.2 million in grant payments for the year 2025, filing shows foundation’s largest single payment of $6.16 million not to a directly named charity but …
articles.summary: The Pichai Family Foundation, established by Google CEO Sundar Pichai and based in San Francisco, reported nearly $9.2 million in grant payments for the
articles.body: The Pichai Family Foundation, established by Google CEO Sundar Pichai and based in San Francisco, reported nearly $9.2 million in grant payments for the 2025 tax year, according to its latest IRS filing. But its biggest payment did not go to a directly named charity. Around $6.16 million was directed to the GS Donor Advised Philanthropy Fund for Wealth Mgmt in Albany, New York, the filing shows. The payment accounted for nearly two-thirds of the foundation's total grant spending for the year and was listed as general operating support. The filing is available through ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer.Pichai Family Foundation's donation in 2025The foundation's second-largest payment was around $2 million to the Castilleja School Foundation in Palo Alto. Other recipients included organisations working in education, healthcare, food security and children's welfare. Second Harvest of Silicon Valley received approximately $450,000, while Boys & Girls of the Peninsula was awarded around $125,000. Doctors Without Borders and UNICEF USA each received about $100,000. The foundation also made grants to Peninsula Bridge and Pratham USA, both associated with educational initiatives.Other payments included around $50,000 to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco, $25,000 to the Global Fund for Children and approximately $15,000 to Aarti for Girls. The 2025 filing listed 11 grant payments in total.Why Pichai’s family foundation sent $6.16 million to a donor-advised fundA donor-advised fund, or DAF, is a charitable giving arrangement that allows donors to contribute money to a fund and recommend grants to eligible organisations over time. The sponsoring organisation retains legal control of the assets and handles the subsequent grantmaking. This means the $6.16 million payment recorded in the Pichai Family Foundation's filing does not identify the final charities that may eventually receive the money. The filing records the transfer to the fund, but does not disclose the fund's subsequent distribution of those assets.The latest figures also point to an increase in the foundation's reported grantmaking. Its 2020 filing recorded seven grants worth approximately $510,000. The available 2022 record showed 11 grants totalling $2.6 million, followed by $4.2 million across 12 grants in 2023 and $6.3 million across 11 grants in 2024.The foundation also made a similar payment of approximately $5.1 million to the same Albany-based donor-advised fund in 2024. Together, the two payments amount to nearly $11.3 million. Across available filings for 2020, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, the foundation reported 52 grants worth approximately $22.9 million, reaching 19 distinct recipients, according to figures compiled by OpenGrants from IRS electronic filing data.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: How the Iran war is reshaping the US military presence in the Middle East
articles.summary: Experts say fallout from the war and domestic opposition could force a smaller permanent presence in the Middle East.
articles.body:
The United States military presence across the Middle East is sprawling.

There are as many as 50,000 US troops and about 19 major military installations in the region, as well as assets spread across countries such as Bahrain, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.

But experts warn that the US-Israel war on Iran has exposed vulnerabilities in protecting Washington’s military assets in the region, leading some to speculate that a downsizing may occur once the war is over.

Michael O’Hanlon, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington-based think tank, is among those who expect the US to eventually scale back its military presence in the Middle East.

“I think we will go smaller, more dispersed, more hardened, and generally further away from Iran — but not in each and every case,” O’Hanlon said.

As the war enters its 10th month on Saturday, the damage inflicted on US installations in the Middle East could one day translate into a strategic shift — not just for the US but for other countries that have been shaped by its military presence as well.

One of the long-term obstacles to maintaining the US military presence will be the cost of repairs.

Repairing damaged infrastructure on US bases in the region could cost $9.4b, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington, DC-based think tank.

Hundreds of structures on US bases have been damaged by Iranian attacks since February 28, when the war began.

One of those bases was in Bahrain, home to the US Naval Forces Central Command and its Fifth Naval Fleet. The US has established a naval command presence in the country as far back as 1948.

But according to a report from the Congressional Research Service, the base — called Naval Support Activity (NSA) Bahrain — “sustained serious damage” in the early days of the Iran war. It estimated the cost of repairing the base at more than $400m.

Other US military assets in the region have also been impacted by the war .

In September, a Department of Defense inspector general report found the US had lost dozens of aircraft during the war, among them attack helicopters and sophisticated fighter jets like the F-35A and the F-15E.

By October, the total cost of the Iran war reached more than $47bn, according to Pentagon figures.

Rebuilding the US bases is unlikely until the Iran war is over, according to Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the Defense and Security Department at CSIS.

“If the war ends with some sort of ceasefire or we get to a place where it’s somewhat stable,” Cancian said, “then you will see some reduction in US forces and reduction of the surge forces certainly and some rebuilding of the bases.”

But Cancian expects that the US will not rebuild all the military sites struck by Iran.

He pointed to the Bahrain headquarters of the Fifth Naval Fleet and the Combined Air Operations Center at Al Udeid airbase in Qatar as examples.

Some military facilities, he explained, will likely be moved underground to protect against aerial attack. Others may be relocated further from the Gulf, to places such as Israel or Jordan.

Major bases like those in Bahrain or Qatar were a liability because “they are right within the range of Iranian missiles and drones”, according to Kelly Grieco, a defence policy expert and senior fellow at the Stimson Center, a global security think tank.

But simply moving bases further away will not protect them in the long term. Grieco pointed out that Iran keeps improving its ability to reach longer-distance targets with drones and missiles.

One alternative to rebuilding bases, she said, would be instead to cultivate access to a network of airstrips and temporary bases in the Middle East that could be used if another conflict erupts.

In the Iran war, for instance, the US has relied extensively on facilities like Israel’s Ben Gurion airport for refuelling combat aircraft.

“What mattered more was access to places and the ability to move around those places, more than having a permanent operating facility,” Grieco said.

Experts say downsizing the US military presence in the Middle East has been a goal across several administrations.

President Donald Trump, for instance, has completed troop withdrawals from Syria and Iraq since the start of his second term in 2025. His predecessor, Joe Biden, also oversaw the US military pullout from Afghanistan in 2021.

But practical realities — including the emergence of new conflicts involving the US — have put that aspiration of a large-scale drawdown out of reach.

“The Biden administration wanted to reduce the force posture. The Trump administration wanted to reduce the force posture,” Cancian said. “They haven’t been able to, and it’s not clear they will be able to.”

Allies and adversaries alike also help to determine the heft of the US military presence, he added.

“The world gets a vote, and even if the administration wants to reduce the force posture, it may not be possible, because of continuing tensions,” Cancian said.

New alliances, however, have emerged that might make certain regional allies less reliant on US military resources.

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, a pact that theoretically commits the countries to come to each other’s aid in case of an attack.

Experts say the deal could trigger a regional realignment away from the US and its military might.

Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan could potentially wield formidable force : Together, they have more than 1.4 million active military personnel, own thousands of tanks and military aircraft and spend more than $124bn on their combined defence budget.

The pact is also likely to expand to include Egypt and Syria, further increasing its resources.

Such agreements might prove to be the first step in diversifying each country’s military strategy beyond their cooperation with the US, according to Grieco.

“The region had already been engaged in strategic diversification before this war started,” she said. “The real question moving forward is: Will they decide to pursue greater strategic dependence, or slowly decrease their dependence on the US for security?”

In the US, voter frustration could also disincentivise any effort to rebuild military installations in the Middle East.

The Iran war and US support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza have proven to be unpopular among the American public.

This month, for instance, the research firm Ipsos and the Reuters news agency found that 71 percent of Americans wanted Congress to end the war on Iran.

The conflict proved especially unpopular at the polls, with Trump’s Republican Party losing key races in the 2026 midterms to Democrats who were vocal in their opposition.

There was even backlash from within Republican ranks. Vice President JD Vance, who once touted his opposition to foreign wars, blamed the Iran conflict for his party’s poor showing in the midterm elections.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so,” Vance wrote on social media. “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Both parties are leaning away from a foreign interventionist stance, according to Grieco.

Although politicians are split over topics like US support for Israel, Grieco has observed that there is an overall inclination to extricate the US military from the Middle East.

“For most Americans, they’ve looked at the region since 1990 or 1991 and seen we are constantly conducting these interventions,” Grieco said. “None of them have gone well.”

articles.title: Former Florida mayor urges American Jews to fight back against rising antisemitism
articles.summary: In "The Jewish Fight for America," Gabe Groisman says forces on the left and right are trying to distance American Jews from Israel and unlearn Zionism.
articles.body: As antisemitism surges across the United States and around the world in the wake of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, massacre, policy strategist and public speaker Gabe Groisman is urging American Jews to stand their ground and fight for the future of their community — and the soul of the nation. In his new book, "The Jewish Fight for America," Groisman, a former mayor of Bal Harbour, Florida, explores the history of American Jews and their contributions to the country, arguing that despite rising antisemitism, they should confront the tide of hate and stand firm in their rightful place. "The first fight we have to take on here in the U.S. is to strengthen the community, to try to teach our brothers and sisters about who we are as a people," Groisman told Fox News Digital. "Then we can get to the part of why the Land of Israel is important to us, why Jewish sovereignty over the Land of Israel, which is the State of Israel today, is an integral part of who we are as Jews in America or anywhere in the world." CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND One of the book’s chapters opens with quotes from Genesis. Groisman explained that powerful forces are seeking to distance American Jews from Israel. It begins with the Bible and the words of God himself," Groisman said. He noted that only 26% of American Jews say they believe in "God as described in the Bible," per a Pew Research Center study published in May 2021. According to the study, another 50% believe in some other spiritual force. "Most American Jews don't hold a biblical or Judeo-Christian understanding of God, and I think that's a huge reason why most don't look to the Bible for their connection to the land," said Groisman. "When they are asked to defend their connection to the Land of Israel or to the State of Israel, they can’t begin to respond in a proper way because they don’t believe in God," he added. Groisman has practiced law for more than 20 years, litigating cases nationwide and participating in legal challenges on behalf of the Jewish community. A NEW CHAPTER FOR AMERICA’S 250TH: 'J250' INITIATIVE PUTS JEWISH CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE SPOTLIGHT During his tenure as mayor, Groisman passed what he describes as the nation's first anti-Israel boycott ordinance, as well as the first municipal ordinance adopting a definition of antisemitism. We need to understand that this community has been here since before day one and has played integral roles in this country. The religious liberties established in this country from the beginning were meant to benefit groups explicitly like the Jews, who were here from day one," he said. For American Jews, Groisman said, the solution lies in helping young people reconnect with their identity. He argued that a strong sense of identity and purpose, rooted in their Jewish religion and national heritage, can help them become confident American Jews and thrive in the United States. "America is not about freedom from religion; it’s about freedom of religion. You are allowed to be who you are as an American and still be as American as everybody else," he said. In his book, Groisman examines developments over the past several years that he believes have contributed to the surge in antisemitism, including the rise of intersectionality and critical race theory on the left and their growing influence in academic and intellectual circles, which he says have received significant funding from foreign actors. He argued that foreign actors unable to defeat the United States militarily seek to weaken it by creating internal divisions, with antisemitism serving as "a useful tool" in that effort. "When we saw actors in this country, in the aftermath of Oct. 7 and even before Israel responded in Gaza, being coordinated and directed by foreign actors in the United States, all the way down to small chapters on college campuses across the country, that requires years and years of coordination," he said. articles.title: China probes Shanghai party chief Chen Jining over corruption
articles.summary: Chen is the fourth Politburo member to be probed since last year in a campaign that has targeted top Chinese leaders.
articles.body:
China’s anticorruption watchdog has launched an investigation into the top Chinese Communist Party leader in Shanghai and member of the elite Politburo, Chen Jining, according to state media.

The 62-year-old, who is the fourth member of the top leadership body to be probed since last year, is suspected of “severe violations of discipline and laws”, the Xinhua news agency reported. The phrase is a common euphemism for corruption.

As part of President Xi Jinping’s widening anticorruption campaign , three Politburo members from the 24-member body have already been removed in its current term, which began in 2022, including General Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission that oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.

Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, said Chen’s investigation was part of an “unprecedented pattern”.

“The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping’s anticorruption campaign has no limits,” he said.

Chen earned a doctorate in environmental engineering at Imperial College London and rose through the ranks at China’s elite Tsinghua University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister before becoming the mayor of Beijing. In 2022, he joined the Politburo as the party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.

The post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions, often serving as a springboard to top leadership roles. Xi briefly served in the role in 2007 before joining the Politburo’s Standing Committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.

China’s second-ranking official, Prime Minister Li Qiang, as well as Vice President Han Zheng, also held the Shanghai post before moving into central leadership roles.

In a separate development, Liu Min, a senior official at the Ministry of Science and Technology, has also been placed under investigation for suspected “serious violations of party discipline and national laws”.

articles.title: Dancing with the Stars: Irish reality star Maura Higgins reaches final
articles.summary: The final will be shown on ABC and Disney+ in the US at 20:00 local time, with no option for people here in the UK to watch live.
articles.body:
Maura Higgins is arguably Love Island's biggest success story.

Since leaving the villa in Majorca, Higgins maintained a high profile in the UK, Ireland and across the Atlantic where she has presented Love Island: Aftersun in the US, and was runner up in The Traitors US.

While she failed to find love with Curtis Pritchard in the 2019 series, she may have picked up a few of the ballroom dancer's moves.

The Irish reality TV star has cha cha cha'd her way to the final of Dancing With the Stars on US television, where she will compete with her professional dance partner Mark Ballas, son of Strictly head judge Shirley Ballas.

From County Longford, there'll be a flavour of Ireland in her dances for the final.

In a video posted to the programme's Instagram page, traditional Irish music can be heard while Higgins and Ballas rehearse.

It will not be the first time on the show Higgins has paid homage to her homeland after she and Ballas performed a Paso Doble to Dropkick Murphy's song I'm Shipping up to Boston.

The former Love Island contestant booked her slot in the finale by earning a perfect 30 out of 30 for her samba and a 29 for her Viennese waltz in last week's semi-final, which saw Grey's Anatomy and Glee star Harry Shum Jr lose the public vote.

The show, hosted by Fresh Prince of Bel-Air star Alfonso Ribeiro and Emmy winning dancer Julianne Hough, features a judging panel of three, made up of Derek Hough, Carrie Ann Inaba and former Strictly Come Dancing regular Bruno Tonioli.

Higgins and Ballas will compete for the Len Goodman Mirrorball trophy.

Goodman, who died in April 2023 , had been one of the regular judges on the show, following his 12-year stint on Strictly.

The pair will face off against actress Tatyana Ali, Paralympian Ezra Frech, comedian Connor Wood and Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn.

Higgin's US career has taken off following her time on the US version of The Traitors which saw her go all the way to the final as a faithful.

She ultimately trusted traitor Rob Rausch, narrowly missing out on victory.

But she did get a Birkin bag from Rausch by way of an apology for betraying her.

In the UK, Higgins has appeared on I'm a Celebrity, Dancing on Ice and Cooking with the Stars, as well as fronting Glow Up Ireland for RTÉ in 2021.

She has also been announced as the presenter of a reboot of Blind Date, due to launch next year.

The three-hour Dancing With the Stars final will be shown on ABC and Disney+ in the US at 20:00 EST.

articles.title: California dad falls 500 feet to his death after saving son on icy mountain trail
articles.summary: Guillermo Batres, 44, fell about 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell after rescuing his son, leaving family grieving as a GoFundMe nears $25,000.
articles.body: While hiking Mount Baden-Powell in the San Gabriel Mountains, a California father fell roughly 500 feet to his death after helping his son recover from a slip on the ice. Guillermo Alejandro Batres, 44, lost his life while attempting to summit the 9,407-foot peak on Sunday, according to a GoFundMe set up by his niece, Jennifer. After October, conditions on Mount Baden-Powell can shift rapidly from a standard, intermediate hike to hazardous winter terrain, as snow and ice quickly accumulate along its shaded, steep slopes. Batres' son slipped on the ice and as Batres went to pull him up, that's when he fell himself, the family said. MOUNTAIN CLIMBER SURVIVES TERRIFYING 500-FOOT FALL IN CALIFORNIA'S SIERRA NEVADA, NIGHT STRANDED ON LEDGE "As Guillermo tried to help him up, he slipped on ice and fell approximately 500 feet down a steep gulch. Guillermo died in the fall, leaving his family shocked, grieving, and facing an unimaginable loss," Jennifer wrote in the GoFundMe description. As of Tuesday morning, the online fundraiser had pulled in more than $25,000 toward its $40,000 goal. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner ruled Batres' death an accident and said he died from blunt force injuries. FAMILY'S SPRING BREAK HIKE TURNS INTO LIFE-OR-DEATH RESCUE AFTER PARENT FALLS 70 FEET OFF UTAH CLIFF Batres had a following on Instagram, where he frequently posted about his passion for running and hiking. In July 2025, Batres became a certified ultrarunning coach — a specialist who helps runners build the endurance needed for races longer than a traditional 26.2-mile marathon, which can stretch for multiple days and stretch for up to 100 miles. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP An avid hiker and outdoorsman, Batres also founded Clean Plug Sneaker Cleaner, his own brand of shoe-cleaning products.

articles.title: Suicide: Father wants education to help men and boys 'in crisis'
articles.summary: Seamus Waites says there was "no warning" before his 22-year-old son died by suicide 10 years ago.
articles.body:
A father whose son died by suicide on the day after his 22nd birthday has called for more education on how men and boys can seek help during a mental health crisis.

Seamus Waites said there was "no warning sign whatsoever" before his son Thomas took his own life in May 2016, just hours after he went out to celebrate with friends.

Waites, who has since become a grief counsellor, said when men reach crisis point they "do not understand the emotions that they're feeling, they become totally overwhelmed and don't know where to go".

Suicide remains the leading cause of death for boys and men aged under 50 in Northern Ireland - of the 262 people who took their own lives last year, 203 were male.

Thomas Waites was a talented young athlete from Magherafelt, County Londonderry, who had represented Ireland in amateur boxing and had a promising career outside the ring ahead of him.

"He had just landed himself a great job, he had bought the car he had always wanted," his father recalled, adding that "from the outside" nothing appeared to be wrong.

Waites went to the gym with his son on the morning of his birthday and said "everything was normal" when Thomas went out that night to celebrate.

The following day, when Thomas did not return home for a barbeque organised in his honour, his father went to check on him at a friend's house.

It was believed Thomas was upstairs listening to music, but when Seamus Waites went into the bedroom, he discovered his son's body.

"You can imagine the shock that it had on us," he said, adding that moment changed his family's lives forever.

Thomas had no known contact with mental health services and even now, a decade on, his family still does not have a full explanation for his death.

"Anybody who takes their own life is in intolerable pain," his father said.

"There needs to be more education around how men cope and how men can reach out."

Waites, who experienced his own mental health struggles after his son's death, now works with an organisation which helps families bereaved by suicide.

"There is an awful stigma about men and how we regulate our emotions," he told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme .

"We are brought up in such a way where we, our families, prepare us to be mentally strong, to be the person that everybody else leans on."

He added the "stigma and shame" associated with not living up to that role meant some men find it difficult to reach out for help when they are in crisis.

On Tuesday night, he will join about 130 families in Ballymena, County Antrim, for a Ceremony of Lights event where their loved ones will be remembered.

Although suicide figures fluctuate each year, the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (Nisra) monitors trends by tracking the average every three years.

This method of calculation shows an increasing pattern, with suicides rising by a quarter in less than a decade.

In 2017, the average number of registered suicides stood at just over 204 deaths per year (over the three-year reporting period).

By last year, that number had risen to average of almost 258 deaths per year.

The annual suicide figure for 2025, disregarding averages, stood at a total of 262 deaths, 77.5% of which were men and boys.

Mental health champion, Prof Siobhan O'Neill, described the latest figures as deeply concerning.

"Suicide loss is absolutely devastating," she told Good Morning Ulster.

"It changes people's lives forever in a way that's very different to any other sort of bereavement or grief."

O'Neill said not enough was being done address the issue and that patients must be able to access immediate help from "the first time" they report suicidal thoughts.

"Sadly, we can see now when we look at those three-year rolling averages, that we're seeing a rise in Northern Ireland.

"And that's different from the other UK regions and the Republic of Ireland where they're seeing either a flat line or a trend towards a decrease in suicides."

O'Neill said mental health services were underfunded per capita in Northern Ireland compared to England and the Republic of Ireland.

She added authorities must examine what is "driving" the rise in Northern Ireland, arguing there has been a failure to tackle poverty, which is linked high suicide rates.

Pointing to Nisra's figures, she said that nearly a "third of those deaths are in deprived areas".

Waites said people bereaved by suicide are also at higher risk of a mental ill health and it helps to have someone to "navigate you through" those feelings.

"The pain is indescribable and I basically watched my family go through the most tormented emotional feelings that I've ever seen a human being going through," he said.

He said that his initial concern after his son's death was how he was going to support his family.

"I very much took it upon my own shoulders to do that, but at the same time, I was grieving as well."

Waites, originally from London, explained that about a year had passed after his son's death when he "crashed" emotionally.

"At one stage I actually thought that I was losing my mind," he recalled.

"My wife actually turned around and said to me: 'You need help'."

Having benefited from counselling, Waites now works with the Bereaved by Suicide service which is run by the Northern Health Trust.

It provides one-to-one counselling in Ballymena, Cookstown and Coleraine and group sessions led by trained counsellors who have lost loved ones to suicide.

"I didn't realise that there was help out there," he said.

Waites said although his life will never be the same, he wanted to use his "lived experience" to ease the grief of others and help them "learn to live alongside it".

articles.title: Body washed ashore in Oregon identified as former city councilor missing since September plane crash
articles.summary: Human remains that washed ashore on the Oregon coast were identified as Ralph H. Busby III, whose plane crashed into the Pacific Ocean in September.
articles.body: Human remains that washed ashore along the Oregon coast last week have been identified as a 78-year-old former city councilor whose small plane crashed into the Pacific Ocean in September. The Oregon State Medical Examiner's Office confirmed on Monday that the remains were identified as Ralph H. Busby III, FOX12 Oregon reported. Busby served on the Newport City Council from 2013 to 2017, the city said in a statement posted to its Facebook page on Monday. Busby was the lone occupant of a twin-engine Beechcraft B95 that crashed about a mile west of Nye Beach near Newport shortly before 12:45 p.m. on Sept. 21, according to the U.S. Coast Guard Northwest District. 4 FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS FOUND DEAD AFTER SMALL PLANE GOES DOWN OFF THE BAHAMAS Eyewitness Yoshio Abe, who was fishing just south of the Yaquina Head Lighthouse, told the outlet in September that he noticed the plane flying unusually low, about 20 feet above the water, in a strange flight pattern before it hit the ocean. "Within three minutes the head went down, and in 10 seconds the whole thing went down," Abe said. The Coast Guard deployed a helicopter and search-and-rescue boats and covered around 124 square miles before suspending the search later that night. The body was discovered in the surf near Yaquina Head Lighthouse on Nov. 15, Oregon State Police said. Weather and hazardous surf conditions kept state police and U.S. Coast Guard crews from recovering the remains for three days until the body washed ashore. FLORIDA LEARJET CRASH INVESTIGATORS DIG UP ENGINE PIECE AFTER PILOTS WARNED OF ROUGH WEATHER AHEAD Oregon State Police told the outlet that the National Transportation Safety Board has been notified as investigators continue looking into the Sept. 21 crash. After officials identified the remains, the City of Newport posted its statement extending condolences to Busby's wife, Sharon, his family and friends. City officials noted his work on the Budget, Airport and Vision 2040 advisory committees and his advocacy for the Newport Municipal Airport. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "His dedication to the community and his willingness to give his time and experience helped guide Newport's future," the city said in its statement. "We are grateful for Ralph's years of service to Newport and the lasting impacts he made on our community," it continued.

articles.title: Jersey fire service draft plan warns of flood and wildfire risks
articles.summary: The fire service has launched a public consultation on its draft a plan up to 2030
articles.body:
Flooding, severe weather and wildlife are among risks outlined by the States of Jersey Fire and Rescue Service (SJFRS) in its draft plan.

The service has invited islanders to have their say on "priorities for keeping Jersey safe over the next four years" during an eight-week consultation.

The plan outlines risks facing Jersey and how SJFRS should use its people and resources to prevent emergencies, protect Islanders and respond when incidents happen, it said.

Ben Elliott, station commander, said Jersey was a "safe place" but the service faced changing risks and wanted to ensure its priorities "reflect what matters most to the community".

"I would encourage Islanders to take just ten minutes to complete the consultation and tell us what they think," he added.

"Your feedback will help shape how we prevent, prepare for and respond to emergencies over the next four years."

The service has drafted eight objectives up to 2030, asking islanders to share their views on whether they are the right priorities and highlight any omissions.

These risks include flooding, severe weather and wildfire, while road traffic collisions and other major incidents are also outlined.

Also among priorities were higher-risk buildings and households, new technology and building methods, as well as growing demand on the service.

The consultation closes on 15 January 2027.

articles.title: Army to detonate lead explosives in Iowa on Wednesday morning as officials insist the plan is necessary
articles.summary: The Army will detonate a large cache of lead azide explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant at 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, officials said, insisting that the plan is the best and only option because the chemical is unstable and at risk of exploding on its own.
articles.body: The Army will detonate a large cache of lead azide explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant at 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, officials said, insisting that the plan is the best and only option because the chemical is unstable and at risk of exploding on its own. A host of federal officials — from the Army, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and other agencies — said at a news conference Tuesday that extensive safety precautions are being taken to protect the public. The detonation is expected to send a plume of lead dust southwest across Iowa and into neighboring Missouri, according to the Army’s forecast map. Officials recommended that anyone in the immediate vicinity evacuate. The plan has prompted widespread distress and confusion among local residents, many of whom say they have not had enough time to prepare for the possible health and environmental consequences. Lead is a potent neurotoxin and there is no safe level of exposure. The 68 drums of the deteriorating, toxic lead azide, once used to make bombs, are stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The Army has said it needs to detonate them because the chemical has undergone a process of “recrystallization,” making it highly unstable and dangerous. The cold weather increases the risk of a spontaneous explosion, officials said. “It’s just a matter of time when we have an uncontrolled detonation,” ATF Director Robert Cekada said. “It’s not a matter if, it’s a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be.” In response to a lawsuit challenging the detonation plan, a federal appeals court on Monday gave the Army the green light to proceed. Army officials said they discovered the problem following an inspection in March. “This is not something that just happened overnight. We’ve been really working hard to figure out the best way to get this done as safely as possible for the surrounding communities and our personnel here,” Cekada said. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the Army and other federal partners were taking “unprecedented, innovative” measures to contain the blast, with the goal of keeping as much lead dust as possible within the ammunition plant site. In its communications about the detonation plan, the Army has described a two-story structure of “HESCO” barriers — modular, collapsible structures filled with sand — built around the blast site. The Army also said it would saturate the sand and apply a mist as the blast went off. Telle described additional measures on Tuesday: The Army plans to use a “water wall” to help absorb small particles, he said, as well as foam barriers to help absorb the blast and “state-of-the-art gel blocks in huge quantities.” It wasn’t immediately clear if those new strategies were added to the plan recently or if the Army had intended to use them all along. The Army did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to emergency permitting documents submitted to the EPA, the Army thinks chunks of concrete could land up to 3,000 feet away from the blast site and smaller objects could go farther. The blast is expected to leave a crater 38 feet wide and about 5 feet deep. Telle said the Army had explored other options to neutralize the lead azide but determined that none were safe. “We wanted to prevent having a high-order detonation because there is risk associated with that,” he said. “However, we were never able to find a viable alternative.” The Army at one point did pursue a plan to neutralize the chemical a different way, which would have avoided an explosion. It awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, which uses a chemical product that dissolves in water and can be sprayed onto the explosives to neutralize them, company CEO Valentine Nzengung told NBC News. But the Army canceled the contract shortly after initiating it, Nzengung said. The New York Times first reported on the contract. Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the Army’s 71st Explosive Ordnance Disposal Group, said Tuesday that this neutralization approach proved to be unsafe. “The barrels of lead azide have deteriorated rapidly over the past eight months. We’ve observed a significant accumulation of crystallized lead azide on the exterior of the barrels, including the barrel lids,” he said. “So it prevents those barrels from being able to be moved. It prevents us from removing the lids of the barrels.” Nzengung, who is also a professor of environmental geochemistry at the University of Georgia, said he did not understand the Army’s conclusion. “We have performed the same exercise before, with the same lead azide in the same packaging and storage deemed unstable. So I don’t understand the assessment,” he said. “If it doesn’t work, I would not be alive ... I have opened more lead azide barrels that are deemed unstable than anybody using a chemical method.” Nzengung added, however, that he did not have the latest details about the degradation from the Army. The weather conditions expected Wednesday morning make it an optimal time for the planned blast, officials said. “The forecast weather patterns are ideal to protect public health and safety across the region,” Telle said. An Army-produced map indicates that the lead dust could be deposited at meaningful concentrations about 40 miles away, toward the community of Farmington and into northeastern Missouri. The Army described the evacuation zone as a “5-mile cone extending southwest” of the ammunition plant. “If there are women who are pregnant, children under the age of 6 or children in general, and individuals who may have chronic disease, you definitely want to be out of that area,” said Sean Kaufman, the principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Department of Health and Human Services. “I would evacuate that area.” Short-term hotel lodging is being provided for Middletown residents and others in the evacuation zone through Friday, the Army said. Anyone who remains in the area is urged to stay indoors. Those residents “will certainly hear and potentially feel with the rattling windows,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command. Richard Fordyce, a U.S. Agriculture Department undersecretary, said that approximately 350 farms could be impacted, based on the anticipated direction of the plume. Any concerned residents in Iowa, Illinois and Missouri can ask for their property to be examined for lead contamination, officials said. “If you want your home sampled, your property sampled, your school sampled, you will get that sample,” said Tom Croci, the EPA’s associate administrator for national security and operations coordination. Once Army and contractor cleanup personnel are allowed to re-enter the facility following the detonation, they are expected to spend up to three months remediating the site. According to the Army’s permit, workers might have to move as much as 13 tons of fencing, sand and other debris to a hazardous waste facility. Cleanup crews will wear full-body Tyvek safety suits and a respirator, the documents say. Lead azide, once commonly used in military explosives, was phased out about 15 years ago, Cekada said, “because of how sensitive it is and how difficult it is to maintain in storage and also in transportation.” The nation’s stockpile, previously spread across multiple locations, was moved to the Iowa plant in 2009, he added.
