articles.title: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
articles.summary: An alert issued on Tuesday warns of an increased risk of sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff.
articles.body:
The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.

An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations.

Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.

In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot.

Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.

The joint alert between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.

It also suggested that companies install visible protective security measures "such as CCTV, secure entrances and robust access controls" to "deter hostile activity". These security measures should be "actively promoted... without giving away information that could be used to plan an attack".

When it comes to personal security, any staff members - not just those at the top - should "remain alert to their surroundings, avoid predictable routines where practicable, and consider how personal information, movements and behaviours could be used to build a picture of them, their role and their organisation".

Leaders should ensure their staff know how to manage their personal security, and know what to do if they notice anything suspicious or concerning.

The government said it will give closed-door threat briefings to critical national infrastructure and defence sector CEOs in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who co-authored last year's Strategic Defence Review, said the latest warning was "significant but not new" and the relevant companies will be "quite savvy" about the risks of cyber attacks.

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One that while there had been a recent "uptick" of these kinds of attacks across Europe, "we are not expecting an epidemic".

"These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.

Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face".

Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".

articles.title: A Texas cliff long overlooked as a possible hunting site has yielded evidence that Indigenous communities drove bison over its edge repeatedly across 3,000 years, making it only the state's second verified bison jump
articles.summary: Imagine standing on the edge of a cliff with an entire herd of bison thundering towards you.
articles.body: Imagine standing on the edge of a cliff with an entire herd of bison thundering towards you. These enormous animals, some weighing close to a tonne, are not exactly the easiest creatures to persuade to change direction. Yet, thousands of years ago, Indigenous communities in what is now Texas found a way to do just that, using the landscape to turn a steep drop into a remarkably effective hunting ground.For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Indigenous communities in the Southern Plains used cliffs to hunt bison, a technique more commonly documented in the northern Great Plains. Now, a discovery by Rice University at Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle has provided evidence that hunters repeatedly drove herds over the same cliff for around 3,000 years. The site, known as Nighthawk, is only the second scientifically verified bison jump in Texas, and suggests that a rather significant piece of Indigenous hunting history had been hiding in plain sight.How did a bison jump work?Before getting into the discovery, it helps to understand what archaeologists mean by a bison jump. And no, it does not involve the animals voluntarily taking a leap of faith.According to Wikipedia, Bison jumps were a communal hunting technique in which groups of Indigenous hunters worked together to drive large herds towards a cliff edge. Rather than chasing individual animals with weapons, hunters used their knowledge of the landscape, animal behaviour and coordinated movements to guide an entire herd towards a steep drop. Once the animals fell, many would die from their injuries, while others would be too badly hurt to escape.It was an enormous undertaking that required more than a few people waving their arms and hoping for the best. Different groups had specialised roles. Some hunters located the herds and gradually guided them towards the chosen area. Others waited along the route, emerging from hiding to steer the animals in the right direction. Once the bison had fallen, additional members of the community would kill any surviving injured animals and begin processing the meat, hides, bones and other useful materials.The technique made it possible to secure a large amount of food and raw materials in a single hunting event. It also required considerable cooperation, planning and an understanding of the animals' movements. As August Costa, the lead author of the study and an adjunct lecturer of anthropology at Rice University, explained to Phys.org, large-scale bison hunts were exciting precisely because they required so many people working together.Nighthawk’s geography presented a slightly different challenge from the more familiar bison jumps found further north. The cliff is not simply a straight, concealed drop. It projects outwards like a spur, meaning the animals could potentially see the danger ahead.Researchers believe hunters may have used the shape of the land to guide the bison onto this narrow extension, gradually restricting their options. The team even suggests that people may have created a false barrier using materials such as bison hides, brush or logs to prevent the animals from turning back. Instead of simply stampeding towards an unexpected cliff, the herd may have been funnelled along a route that left it with very few ways out. The researchers compare the arrangement to walking the plank.It is a fascinating possibility, although archaeologists have not yet established exactly how the hunters managed to guide the animals over the edge.What researchers discovered at NighthawkThe Nighthawk site is located beneath a roughly 20-metre-high cliff in Caprock Canyons State Park. Researchers began investigating the area after bison bones started emerging from the eroding ground below the cliff. Alongside hundreds of bones, they found chipped stone tools, projectile points and arrowheads, some of which suggested that the animals had been butchered using stone implements.Initially, archaeologists thought the remains represented evidence of perhaps two separate hunting events. However, the team went further, using radiocarbon dating to establish how old the bones were and whether they belonged to different periods.The findings, published in the journal American Antiquity, revealed at least seven distinct bison kill events spread across approximately 3,000 years. Researchers analysed 27 radiocarbon measurements taken from bison bone collagen and charcoal to establish the timeline.In other words, this was not a group of hunters who stumbled upon a useful cliff once and decided to try their luck again. Different generations returned to the same hunting ground over thousands of years, even as their tools, technologies and ways of life changed.The evidence suggests that the technique survived the transition from stone-tipped spears to bows and arrows, as well as the introduction of pottery in the region. The landscape itself changed considerably, too. Erosion gradually shifted the cliff's jump-off point by approximately the length of a football field. Yet, hunters continued to use the area.Costa told researchers that repeatedly returning to the same location over such an extended period suggested that communities had developed a significant connection with the Nighthawk hunting facility.There may also have been more to these hunts than simply securing the next meal. Costa suggested to Phys.org that large communal hunts could have brought different groups together for ceremonies, trade and celebrations, while strengthening relationships between communities. The researchers believe these gatherings may have served important social and political purposes alongside their practical value.How has this discovery changed what we understand?For years, archaeologists believed that large-scale bison jumps were largely a feature of the northern Great Plains, where several well-documented hunting sites have been discovered. In the Southern Plains, however, the evidence was considerably thinner. Before Nighthawk, the only scientifically verified bison jump in Texas was Bonfire Shelter, a site identified more than 60 years ago.The new discovery challenges the idea that Indigenous communities in the region did not use the technique. In fact, Costa and his colleagues have identified eight potential bison jump sites in and around Caprock Canyons, suggesting that the practice may have been much more widespread than previously understood.So why did it take so long to find them? Part of the problem is where archaeologists have traditionally looked. Hunting sites are often investigated for evidence of human activity, such as tools, shelters and places where people lived. But bison jumps leave much of their evidence beneath cliffs, on steep slopes that would not have been particularly suitable for settlements or campsites.Erosion has also played a role in concealing or destroying archaeological evidence, while several potentially important sites are located on privately owned land that researchers cannot easily access. According to the study, some of the sites had actually been identified decades ago but were never properly investigated or acknowledged as possible bison jumps.As Costa put it, the jump was hidden in plain sight.The research team is now looking beyond Nighthawk to investigate other potential hunting sites across the Southern Plains. Researchers are also analysing ancient bison DNA and the chemical composition of bones and teeth to understand how herds moved across the landscape, what their environment looked like and whether ancient animals were related to the bison living in Caprock Canyons State Park today.There is still plenty to learn about the people who lived across North America thousands of years ago. What might look like an ordinary cliffside today could have once been a carefully chosen hunting ground, visited by generations of people who understood its landscape intimately. And sometimes, the most remarkable archaeological discoveries are not buried beneath ancient cities or elaborate monuments. They are sitting right beneath our feet, waiting for a little erosion to bring them back into view.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Best Buy founder Richard Schulze donates $75 million to two Florida cancer centres, including Moffitt’s largest-ever gift, as he works towards his $1 billion philanthropic pledge
articles.summary: Best Buy founder Richard M.
articles.body: Best Buy founder Richard M. Schulze has committed $75 million to cancer care in Florida, including a $35 million donation to Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa. The contribution marks the largest philanthropic gift in the institution's 40-year history and is intended to help expand hospital capacity and provide more patients with access to clinical trials. For Schulze, whose family has been affected by cancer, the funding is part of a wider programme of charitable giving. His latest commitment also adds to a long-running relationship with Moffitt, where previous donations have helped establish specialist treatment facilities.Richard Schulze splits $75 million donation between two Florida cancer centresAs reported by Moffitt Cancer Center, the two donations were announced on November 18 by Richard M. Schulze Family Foundation. As reported, Lee Health, based in Fort Myers, will receive $40 million, while Tampa's Moffitt Cancer Center has been allocated $35 million. Both contributions have been described as the largest charitable gifts in the respective organisations' histories.The larger share will go towards Lee Health's plans to develop its cancer services in Southwest Florida. The funding is intended to support the expansion of the health system's oncology capabilities, including the recruitment of specialist doctors, wider access to advanced treatments and stronger clinical research programmes.Recently, the contribution also comes with a change to the institute's name. Lee Health's existing Cancer Institute will become the Lee Health R.M. Schulze Cancer Institute, recognising the family's financial commitment. The donation is expected to provide a starting point for a separate $100 million fundraising campaign aimed at developing cancer care across the region. Lee Health has also said it plans to commit more than $100 million of its own money to the wider expansion.Moffitt receives its largest donation in four decadesReportedly, at Moffitt Cancer Center, the $35 million contribution will be used to complete two unfinished floors at Moffitt McKinley Hospital. The facility, which opened in 2023, was designed with additional space that could be developed as demand for treatment increased. It initially began operating with 80 staffed inpatient beds.The expansion will add 32 beds on one floor for people requiring specialised cancer treatment and surgery. The other will house a dedicated clinical trial and infusion unit, providing space for patients receiving experimental or emerging therapies that can involve lengthy visits and periods of medical observation.The additional facilities are expected to increase the hospital's capacity and make it easier for patients to access clinical trials. Moffitt has also identified growing patient demand and Florida's rising cancer burden as reasons for expanding its services. Its leadership expects the development to help address pressure on existing beds and reduce waiting times.Patrick Hwu, Moffitt's president and chief executive said, “This extraordinary gift will have an immediate and lasting impact on cancer patients across Florida and beyond.”Richard Schulze adds another $35 million to his long-running Moffitt partnershipThe latest Moffitt donation is not the foundation's first major investment in the centre. Earlier contributions helped establish the Richard M. Schulze Family Foundation Outpatient Center at the McKinley campus and the Richard M. Schulze Family Foundation Proton Center, which provides access to proton therapy.The proton centre opened in July 2026 at Speros, Moffitt's 775-acre life sciences campus in Pasco County. With the latest $35 million contribution, the foundation's total support for Moffitt has reached nearly $60 million. The centre has described the Schulze family as one of its most significant philanthropic partners.Cancer has also been a personal concern for Schulze. In his remarks announcing the donation, he said the disease had affected his family and was a major reason behind his support for organisations working to improve treatment options. His wife, Sandy, died in 2001 from mesothelioma, a cancer associated with asbestos exposure, according to the foundation's account of his life.Schulze’s $1 billion philanthropic pledge and focus on healthcareSchulze established the Richard M. Schulze Family Foundation in 2004, several years after building Best Buy into a major consumer electronics retailer. In June 2013, he announced his intention to give away $1 billion during his lifetime. The foundation's work covers education, health and medicine, and human and social services, with a particular focus on Minnesota and Florida.The $75 million Florida commitment represents another substantial investment in healthcare under that broader philanthropic plan. Rather than funding a single institution, the latest donations support two separate health systems, one serving the Tampa area and the other focused on Southwest Florida.For Lee Health, the money will help advance a wider cancer institute expansion. At Moffitt, it will go towards completing hospital space intended for additional beds and clinical trial services. Both organisations are now preparing to use the funding to increase their capacity to treat patients.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A former Texas middle school teacher posed as a company trustee and redirected $520,000 in stolen federal tax refunds to his accounts; investigators stopped another $4 million in checks before he pleaded guilty
articles.summary: A former Texas middle school teacher has admitted to laundering $520,000 in stolen federal tax refunds.
articles.body: A former Texas middle school teacher has admitted to laundering $520,000 in stolen federal tax refunds. He pretended to be a company trustee and changed the firm's address so the money would be sent to him. An IRS investigator also stopped him from depositing more than $4 million in extra refund cheques, according to the US Department of Justice.Former Texas teacher admits laundering $520,000 in stolen tax refundsA former middle school teacher in Texas has admitted to stealing $520,000 in federal tax refunds. He did this by pretending to be a company trustee and changing its official business address so the cheques went to him. Jeremy Jarod Jackson, who used to teach at G. W. Carver Middle School in Waco, pleaded guilty to one count of money laundering in federal court. He also admitted to putting the stolen refund cheques into his own bank accounts and spending the cash on personal items and services.The US Department of Justice said an IRS Criminal Investigation agent stopped Jackson from putting more than $4 million in extra stolen refund cheques into his accounts. Jackson now faces up to 10 years in prison for the money laundering crime. Justin R. Simmons, US Attorney for the Western District of Texas, announced the guilty plea on 20 November. According to the department, the stolen federal tax refunds belonged to SWBC Professional Employee Services.How the refund scheme workedAccording to court papers cited by the US Department of Justice, Jackson acted as if he were a trustee for SWBC Professional Employee Services. He then changed the business address for the company to make sure its federal tax refund cheques came to him instead. This address change let him get his hands on cheques worth $520,000 in total. Instead of sending that money to the company, Jackson placed the cheques into bank accounts he controlled and used the money for personal shopping and services.The department said Jackson admitted to all of this as part of his guilty plea. He pleaded guilty to one count of money laundering, admitting he handled cash that came from stolen tax refunds. The case was about much more than the $520,000 Jackson managed to deposit. Court papers also showed that a special agent from IRS Criminal Investigation stopped him from depositing more than $4 million in other stolen refund cheques. That quick action kept a much larger sum of money from ever reaching Jackson's bank accounts. The Department of Justice did not share more details about how the agent found out about the scheme or when the extra cheques were stopped.More than $4 million in cheques stoppedThere was a big gap between the money Jackson took and the amount investigators blocked. He managed to deposit cheques worth $520,000, while the IRS agent stopped more than $4 million in other stolen refund cheques from going into his accounts. These numbers came from federal court details shared by the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Texas. The department called the case a plan to launder more than $500,000 in stolen federal tax refunds.The $4 million sum covers cheques that Jackson was blocked from depositing. It is separate from the $520,000 he admitted taking and putting into his personal accounts. IRS Criminal Investigation, known as IRS-CI, investigated the case with help from the McLennan County Sheriff's Office. The federal agency looks into suspected tax-related money crimes, while local police helped look into what Jackson was doing. The US Department of Justice did not say how long the investigation took or list each individual refund cheque involved. Its statement also did not name the banks or accounts where Jackson put the money.Former teacher faces up to 10 years in prisonJackson's guilty plea means he has admitted to one count of money laundering in federal court. The charge carries a top possible prison term of 10 years, according to the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Texas. A top possible sentence is not the same as a final prison term. The department's statement did not give a sentencing date or say how long prosecutors will ask the judge to give Jackson.Assistant US Attorney Greg Gloff is prosecuting the case. US Attorney Justin R. Simmons shared news of the guilty plea for the Western District of Texas on 20 November 2026. The case focuses on Jackson using a fake identity and a changed business address to steal company tax refunds. Investigators stopped more than $4 million in extra cheques before he could cash them, while Jackson admitted taking and spending $520,000. The Department of Justice has not shared any more news about getting back the money Jackson deposited or whether he will face more charges.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Canadian couple Kevin and Marie Isobel Fraser landed in Vancouver nearly 16 hours late after WestJet blamed a wind event in Minneapolis, and a BC tribunal has now ordered the airline to pay them $2,000
articles.summary: A Canadian couple who arrived in Vancouver nearly 16 hours late have won $2,000 in compensation from WestJet after a British Columbia tribunal rejected
articles.body: A Canadian couple who arrived in Vancouver nearly 16 hours late have won $2,000 in compensation from WestJet after a British Columbia tribunal rejected the airline's argument that strong winds caused the delay. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal (CRT) ruled that WestJet had failed to prove that an unexpected weather event was responsible for the disruption experienced by Kevin and Marie Isobel Fraser. According to CP24, the couple were travelling from Minneapolis to Vancouver on 6 June 2024 when their first flight, which was due to take them to Regina, arrived one hour and 37 minutes late. This caused them to miss their connecting flight, leaving them stuck overnight in a hotel in Regina. WestJet booked the couple onto new flights to Vancouver through Calgary the following day. They eventually reached home almost 16 hours later than planned. However, when the Frasers asked the airline for compensation, WestJet refused to pay.Why WestJet claimed a weather exemptionUnder Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations (APPR), major airlines such as WestJet must pay passengers $1,000 each when a flight disruption makes them arrive at least nine hours late. Airlines can avoid paying this compensation if they prove that the delay was caused by something beyond their control, such as severe weather. They can also claim an exemption for unexpected maintenance work that is strictly needed to keep a plane safe. As reported by CP24, WestJet told the tribunal that the delay qualified for both the safety and weather exemptions. The airline said strong winds in Minneapolis had pushed a luggage belt loader into the aircraft, damaging the net used to secure baggage in the cargo area. WestJet argued that aviation rules do not allow planes to take off unless baggage is properly secured and cannot move during the flight. It said maintenance workers therefore had to repair the damage before the aircraft could depart.Tribunal rejects airline's weather defenceTo support its argument, WestJet gave the tribunal an internal document called a "defect report", which recorded the damage to the aircraft. However, CRT member Deanna Rivers found that the airline's own report did not support its claim that the weather had caused the problem."It shows that on June 6, 2024, the pilot reported that a belt loader had damaged the aft baggage door threshold net while moving away from the aircraft," Rivers wrote in her decision, as quoted by CP24. "The damage affected five lower attachment points on the sill. The report identifies the resolution as replacing the aft baggage door restraint net. This was done in Calgary on June 16, 2024." Rivers noted that the report did not mention wind or bad weather as a reason the aircraft could not leave on time."The defect report identifies the belt loader as the source of the damage but does not mention weather or wind conditions," Rivers' decision reads. "There is also no other documentary evidence connecting the damage to the weather."Equipment handling deemed within airline controlWhen deciding whether WestJet was responsible for the damage caused by the belt loader, Rivers considered earlier decisions by the Canadian Transportation Agency. These rulings say that delays caused by airline staff failing to take proper care remain within the airline's control. Rivers used the same principle when considering the Frasers' case. She found that WestJet could not rely on the safety maintenance exemption to avoid responsibility for damage caused by ground equipment."Here, even if the damage to the baggage net required maintenance before the aircraft could safely operate, WestJet has not established that the damage resulted from an unforeseeable weather event," Rivers stated in the ruling."Rather, the evidence only establishes that a belt loader damaged the net. As WestJet has not proved the damage was outside of its control, I find the resulting delay was within WestJet's control and not required for safety purposes."Full breakdown of the $2,226.92 payoutBecause the couple arrived more than nine hours late and the tribunal found that the delay was within WestJet's control, Rivers ordered the airline to pay Kevin and Marie Isobel Fraser $1,000 each under the APPR. This brought their main compensation award to $2,000. According to CP24, the tribunal also ordered WestJet to repay the couple for other expenses they had paid during the disruption, as well as the costs of bringing their case. These included $35.28 for taxi journeys between the airport and their hotel in Regina. Kevin Fraser was also awarded $51 after being given a lower-class seat on the replacement flights through Calgary. WestJet was also told to repay the couple's $125 fee for filing their case with the Civil Resolution Tribunal, along with $15.64 for sending legal documents to the airline by registered mail. With the $2,000 compensation award and all additional expenses included, WestJet must pay the couple a total of $2,226.92.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Hila Klein announces H3 Podcast exit, says she needs to focus on ‘healing’ and her children
articles.summary: Hila Klein has announced that she is stepping away from the H3 Podcast, putting the planned return of the show in doubt.
articles.body: Hila Klein has announced that she is stepping away from the H3 Podcast, putting the planned return of the show in doubt. On November 23, 2026, she shared the news through the podcast's official Instagram account. Hila said she had tried her best to keep the new show going but could no longer continue while dealing with her personal struggles. She wants to focus on her mental health, healing, and children. Her announcement also drew a response from H3 crew member AB Ayad, who shared his thoughts during a livestream.Hila Klein Explains Why She Is Leaving the New H3 Podcast ShowHila's decision comes after a difficult few weeks for her family and the H3 Podcast team. The trouble began in October when she publicly accused her husband and longtime co-host, Ethan Klein, of having an affair. She said he had been involved with another woman for at least six months.The allegations led to their separation and plans for divorce. Ethan also said he wanted to remove his ownership and financial interests from the podcast and other joint projects. Meanwhile, the H3 crew announced that they would not continue working with him.With Ethan no longer involved, the remaining team appeared ready to build a new show with Hila. A November 13 Instagram photo of Hila with several crew members also showed that they were still in contact.However, Hila has now decided not to continue with the project. In her November 23 statement, she explained how difficult the decision had been."I'm so sorry to share that I've made the difficult decision to stop working on the new show. I truly tried with every ounce of strength I had to make this work, but after everything that has happened, I've come to realize that I can't continue down this path while also giving myself the space I need to heal and protect my mental health."She also made it clear that her children and personal well-being need her attention right now."Right now, I need to focus on myself, my healing, and what's best for me and my kids. I'm devastated that things have come to this."Hila did not hide how much the podcast and its team meant to her. She said she loved the community and considered the crew part of her family. She also thanked viewers for supporting her throughout the years and said she would miss them.Her message makes clear that she is walking away from the new show, although it does not explain what will happen to the remaining crew or whether another version of the podcast could return.AB Ayad Reacts to Hila Klein's Exit and Shares His Thoughts on H3 Podcast's FutureHila's announcement also prompted a reaction from crew member Abdullah Ayad, better known as AB. During a November 23 livestream, he spoke about why the team could not move forward with the planned show.AB suggested that some people involved had made it impossible for the crew to continue working together. He said:"I think there were certain people involved that were never gonna allow us to continue doing the show together…so, yes, to all the haters, you can now tell us all to put the fries in the bag…"His comment suggested that the problems behind the show's uncertain future went beyond Hila's decision to leave. However, he did not name the people he was referring to.AB also praised Hila for trying to keep the project alive despite everything happening in her personal life. He said:"I give Hila a lot of credit that she was able to do what she even did… I was assured that it wasn’t my fault… I don’t know, I don’t know if there’s interest or… I don’t think there’s any reality where…that was my initial thought."AB's comments suggest that he does not see a clear way for the original team to continue the show together.As for Ethan, he had earlier asked people to respect his family's privacy after Hila's allegations became public. He has also said he was working to give up his ownership interests in their joint projects. No confirmed announcement about a new H3 Podcast lineup has followed Hila's November 23 decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Israel’s Ben-Gvir accused of seeking ‘religious war’ over mosque raids
articles.summary: Israeli police have confiscated mosque loudspeakers as far-right lawmakers push legislation to restrict call to prayer.
articles.body:
The recent confiscation of loudspeakers at two mosques in southern Israel is the latest example of an attempt by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir to “ignite a religious war”, parliamentarian Ahmad Tibi has told Al Jazeera.

Tibi said that Ben-Gvir, who oversees Israel’s police, was “exploiting the atmosphere of war” after he ordered the removal of the loudspeakers, which are used to broadcast the Islamic call to prayer.

Israeli police disconnected the speakers at a mosque in the Bedouin town of Hura and removed its sound equipment on Sunday.

Days earlier, police had seized the sound system at al-Dawa Mosque in nearby Tel al-Saba, known in Hebrew as Tel Sheva. Police said they had received repeated noise complaints about both mosques.

Ben-Gvir, a far-right figure known for making anti-Palestinian and anti-Arab statements and celebrating harsh treatment inflicted on Palestinian prisoners, defended the removals, saying that noise levels had been too high.

Tibi, a leader of the Ta’al Party – a member of the Joint List – accused caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of leading a campaign of incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel. Netanyahu has attempted to delegitimise any attempt by the opposition to form a government with the backing of Arab-led parties, accusing the latter of supporting “terrorism”.

Critics – including Palestinian citizens of Israel and Israeli opposition leaders – have linked the comments by Netanyahu and other right-wing politicians, as well as their policies, to recent attacks targeting a mosque and an Arab city in Israel.

Ibrahim al-Asam, a Tel al-Saba resident and activist, disputed the police account, writing on social media that the speaker at al-Dawa Mosque was not loud. He said officers damaged the mosque during the raid and took the recorder connected to its security cameras.

Police said they had issued fines and warned those responsible for the sound system at Tel al-Saba before seizing it. In Hura, they said officers checked the volume at the mosque and found it exceeded the legal limit.

“The mosque is far away and doesn’t bother anyone,” said Atiya al-Asam, who heads the regional council representing Bedouin villages in al-Naqab (Negev) that Israel does not recognise. He called the seizure “an assault on people’s faith, on Islam and Muslims”, and said that police had acted without a court order, calling for the speakers to be returned.

The seizures are a continuation of an ongoing policy.

Israeli authorities took loudspeakers from a mosque in the al-Naqab village of Bir al-Hammam in April and from another in Majd al-Krum, in the northern Galilee region, in June. Authorities also summoned several muezzins – who give the call to prayer – for questioning and had warned mosques they could face fines.

The Palestinian monitoring group Mo’ta recorded at least 38 cases in 2026 in which Israeli authorities invoked noise regulations against mosques, imams, or muezzins in Arab and mixed Arab-Jewish communities in Israel.

But they are also taking place in the occupied West Bank. For example, in December 2025, the Israeli military ordered mosques in Ras Tira, near Qalqilya, to lower the volume of the call to prayer. The army distributed notices saying the sound disturbed nearby illegal Israeli settlements.

Mo’ta has reported attacks on 50 mosques in the occupied West Bank, including 13 cases of arson. In Hebron, the Palestinian Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs said Israeli authorities had prevented the call to prayer at the Ibrahimi Mosque 1,009 times since the start of 2026.

On July 1, Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, voted 50 to 36 in a preliminary reading for a bill that would prohibit mosques from using loudspeakers to broadcast the call to prayer without government permission. The legislation, sponsored by Zvika Fogel of Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power party, did not become law.

Jewish Power said on Monday that it would bring a new version of the bill for a parliamentary vote on Wednesday.

articles.title: Putin says retaliation ‘inevitable’ after Ukraine hit Russian oil plants
articles.summary: Ukrainian attacks subsided after Trump’s mid-October declaration of an energy ceasefire, but picked up again afterwards.
articles.body:
Ukraine has continued its attacks on Russian oil refineries despite requests from US President Donald Trump to withhold them, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said while threatening retaliation.

Putin made the threat on Tuesday, after Kyiv said it would stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow did the same.

Ukrainian attacks subsided after Trump’s mid-October declaration of an energy ceasefire in the conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. But they picked up again in late October.

“We see that the Kyiv regime continues to attack our refining facilities, despite the US president’s appeal and direct request to refrain from such attacks. But the Kyiv authorities are ignoring this advice,” Putin told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin.

“In this regard, I would like to stress that retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable.”

He also told the meeting that he wanted additional security measures for energy facilities.

According to estimates from two industry sources cited by the Reuters news agency, Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October.

Several Russian regions have introduced restrictions on retail sales of petrol and diesel following a renewed spate of Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries, according to local media and authorities.

Putin said that while the situation on the domestic fuel market remained difficult, petrol prices have stabilised after they peaked in October.

Elsewhere, Poland on Tuesday accused Moscow of deliberately violating its airspace when a Russian surveillance drone briefly crossed the border.

Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Abdelaziz Mujahid said the incursion “may also signal that the conflict and these confrontations are widening”.

Moscow on Monday accused Estonia, a NATO and European Union member state, of a range of hostile actions “on the verge of triggering open war”, after Estonia announced the closure of their land border.

In other incidents, Warsaw said three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, and a Russian cargo ship with links to the military was hit by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday in an attack claimed by Ukraine.

On Sunday, Ukraine sank a Russian naval corvette in a Libyan port using maritime drones. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the drone attack was a legitimate act of self-defence, following criticism from Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli.

Additionally, British security officials on Tuesday warned United Kingdom companies providing “material support” for Ukrainian armed forces to brace for Russian sabotage attempts.

Meanwhile, a Russian attack killed two people in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia overnight, Governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Tuesday.

Forty people, including four children, were wounded in the assault, Semikin added. Images and a video on his Telegram account showed a damaged apartment building with its windows blown out and rubble on the ground.

The Interfax news agency, citing Russia’s Defence Ministry, said on Tuesday that the Russian military hit drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine’s Sumy region, also killing a number of servicemen.

articles.title: Twitch streamer Nick Lacy criticises GTA 6’s ‘slow’ story despite giving Rockstar’s gameplay a perfect score
articles.summary: Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy” has given Grand Theft Auto 6's gameplay a perfect 10 out of 10 but was less impressed with its story.
articles.body: Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy” has given Grand Theft Auto 6's gameplay a perfect 10 out of 10 but was less impressed with its story. After completing the game, the CORE member rated its storyline 6.5 out of 10, explaining that the early part felt too slow. However, he said things became much better after reaching around 65-70% of the story. Lacy also praised the game's free roam, side quests and interactions, while pointing out one issue with its heist missions. He shared his thoughts in a livestream clip that surfaced on X on November 22, 2026.Nick Lacy explains why GTA 6's gameplay earned a 10/10 while its story received a lower ratingLacy made it clear that his lower story rating did not mean he disliked the game. In fact, he had plenty of praise for what players can do outside the main missions. He believes the open-world experience has enough activities to keep players busy for a long time.Sharing his overall review, the streamer said:"GTA 6, I will give it a 10 out of 10 game. I will give GTA 6 story a 6.5 out of 10. I think the game and the free roam, the side quests, all of the interactions are crazy. I think there is going to be so much, like, things you can do. There are infinite things that you can find. Online is going to be crazy."However, the story did not hold his attention in the same way throughout the game. Lacy said the first part took too long to pick up before things became more interesting."The story, for me, was a little slow in the beginning, until about the 65-70% mark, then it got really good. I will say - I was a little disappointed in the beginning because of how slow it was, but then it got really, really good at the end."He also had a complaint about the money players receive after completing major heists. articles.summary: The release of an “unknown substance” at a British rap concert this weekend may have been linked to a small number ⁠of robberies at the show, British police said on ​Tuesday.
articles.body: The release of an “unknown substance” at a British rap concert this weekend may have been linked to a small number ⁠of robberies at the show, British police said on ​Tuesday. A major incident was declared by police on Sunday evening after people in the crowd at the Co-op Live arena in Manchester, northern ⁠England, fell ill during ​a ⁠performance by U.S. rapper Don Toliver. Greater Manchester Police said the force had received ⁠nine reports of jewelry being stolen during the ​concert, ⁠adding in a statement that “detectives ‌are exploring the possibility that release of the substance could be linked.” Assistant Chief Constable Tom ‌Harding said that “similar robberies have been ‌reported at two European concerts” by Don Toliver and that the police would speak to European law enforcement. “We maintain ⁠our belief that, based on the information available to us now, there is no wider ongoing risk to the public,” Harding said. Around 12,000 people at the concert had to leave the venue and nearly 90 people displayed symptoms ‌believed to be linked to the exposure, the ​police said previously, though just ‌one person was taken to ⁠hospital for further assessment. Toliver, who has ⁠been nominated for several Grammys this year, had been due ‌to perform ​at London’s O2 Arena ‌on Monday but the concert ​was postponed to Dec. 15.

articles.title: Armed men take hostages in Cartagena, one of Colombia’s top tourist destinations
articles.summary: A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding an unknown number of hostages.
articles.body: BOGOTA, Colombia — A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding an unknown number of hostages, Colombian police said. President Abelardo de la Espriella said that the men were “common criminals” who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck. The hostage situation broke out as Colombia is experiencing a wave of attacks by rebel groups on government targets, which has recently spread to urban areas. Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the Exito supermarket, which is located in a mall in Cartagena’s La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have broadcast images of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police. Cartagena is one of Colombia’s main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well preserved 18th century architecture, and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks. Cartagena’s airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in an X message that operations were slowly returning to normal.

articles.title: European leader warns Russian aggression could escalate within weeks or months
articles.summary: Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warns Russia is escalating sabotage, arson and assassination plots against NATO countries that could worsen in weeks.
articles.body: Russia is growing increasingly willing to take risks against NATO countries, with a mounting campaign of sabotage, arson attacks and assassination plots that could escalate within weeks or months, Latvia’s president warned in an interview with Fox News Digital. Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said Western leaders may be underestimating the threat posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin because they fail to fully understand the ideological and historical beliefs driving the Kremlin’s foreign policy. "The appetite for the risk is growing in Russia," Rinkēvičs said. "We see numbers of arson attacks. Some assassination plots. Acts of sabotage." BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT While Russian provocations have so far remained below the threshold that would trigger NATO’s collective defense mechanism under Article 5, Rinkēvičs warned that the situation could deteriorate rapidly. "We see that the number of attacks is rising, but we still see that, at this point, it may change very quickly. It may change maybe in weeks or months or a couple of months' time," he said. The Latvian leader pointed to recent cooperation between Latvian and Estonian intelligence services that he said resulted in arrests in Estonia and prevented an attack against a defense factory. He said the escalating campaign is part of Moscow’s strategy to discourage European countries from continuing to support Ukraine. DENMARK ACCUSES RUSSIA OF PLOTTING TO KILL UKRAINIAN AMERICAN RAPPER ON DANISH SOIL His warning comes just days after President Donald Trump met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, for unprecedented talks that addressed the war in Ukraine and nuclear arms control. On Monday, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Ukraine and NATO countries had already created circumstances in which Moscow could contemplate using nuclear weapons. Medvedev also raised the possibility of a preemptive nuclear strike if Western countries supplied Ukraine with nuclear weapons, while acknowledging that Russia’s nuclear doctrine does not explicitly provide for preventive strikes, Anadolu reported. TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE The West is "too pragmatic" Rinkēvičs argued that Western governments need to reconsider how they interpret Putin’s motivations, suggesting that conventional military, economic and political calculations alone cannot explain the Kremlin’s determination to continue the war. "We are too pragmatic and rational in the West," he said. The Latvian president pointed to Putin’s recent interviews, saying he was struck by the Russian leader’s ideological and religious references, including the historical concept of Russia as the "Third Rome" and its perceived mission to safeguard Christianity. "I think that this kind of belief also drives the war," Rinkēvičs said, describing a "missionary approach that we in the West do not understand because we are too rational and too pragmatic." While Rinkēvičs welcomed continued engagement between Washington and Moscow, he said last week’s summit had not produced a diplomatic breakthrough on Ukraine. "Russia is not willing to end this war," he said. He argued that Moscow is using diplomatic engagement to extend the conflict in the hope of securing further gains both militarily and at the negotiating table. Rinkēvičs said the combination of Russian ideological ambitions, escalating operations against Western countries, upcoming European elections in France, Poland and Italy and political debates in the U.S. could encourage Moscow to continue the fighting. ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH Russia’s escalating threats against NATO The Latvian State Security Service confirmed that eight Latvian nationals were detained in Estonia on Nov. 14, after authorities thwarted an attempted arson attack against Threod Systems, an Estonian drone manufacturer. Estonian security officials attributed the operation to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Estonia subsequently announced it would close its land border with Russia beginning Dec. 1, for at least six months. Russia’s Foreign Ministry responded Monday by accusing Estonia of hostile actions "on the verge of triggering open war," Reuters reported. British security officials also warned Tuesday that companies supporting Ukraine’s military should prepare for potential Russian sabotage attempts after a series of incidents across Europe, The Associated Press reported. The Kremlin has consistently denied conducting sabotage operations against NATO countries. As Fox News Digital reported Monday, new Western intelligence assessments suggest Russia could launch a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon within weeks, potentially threatening thousands of satellites used by the U.S. and its allies. Rinkēvičs said he could not confirm the intelligence assessments but warned that Russia’s pursuit of advanced weapons requires greater Western investment in missile defenses, drones and emerging technologies. "Russia is developing nuclear weapons, developing new technologies and we have to be extremely, extremely careful," he said. However, he cautioned that Moscow has previously overstated its military capabilities. "Whether that weapon in space, nuclear weapon in space is going to be the real thing or just a kind of fake news, remains to be seen," he said. A possible window for peace in 2027 Despite his warnings, Rinkēvičs said an opportunity for meaningful negotiations could emerge next spring or summer if Ukraine withstands Russia’s winter offensive against its civilian and energy infrastructure. "I'm quite confident Ukraine is going to survive. Unfortunately, the big question is at what human cost," he said. Speaking at a U.N. Security Council meeting on Ukraine Monday, Rinkēvičs said Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure had reached their highest level since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022. He warned that millions of Ukrainians face the prospect of spending the winter without electricity, heating or running water. "Winter must never be a weapon of war," he told the council. Rinkēvičs also praised the Oleshky ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump as evidence that diplomatic pressure and political will can produce results. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For now, however, he remains skeptical that Moscow is genuinely seeking peace. "Currently, Russia explores diplomatic efforts in order to prolong the war, not to end the war," he told Fox News Digital. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this article.

articles.title: US Army to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday
articles.summary: Despite alarm about toxic lead, federal officials say destroying the unstable explosives is the safest course of action.
articles.body:
The United States Army has announced it plans to carry out two consecutive, rapid controlled detonations of lead azide in the midwestern state of Iowa at 9am (15:00 GMT) on Wednesday, after a series of postponements.

The announcement on Tuesday comes as controversy continues to swirl around the planned detonation. The explosion risks sending particles of lead, a toxic metal, into surrounding communities.

But military experts warn that the lead azide, a compound used in munitions, will become increasingly unstable in the cold weather, risking an uncontrolled blast.

“Inaction is no longer an option,” Major General Eric Shirley, the army official in charge of the disposal effort, told reporters on Tuesday. “It would be irresponsible for us not to take the determined consensus-based course of action moving forward that has been selected.”

Shirley said the US Army has been working closely with state and federal officials.

The military has also taken a number of steps to mitigate harm to the public, he added. Earthworks had been constructed around the blast site, and cisterns were dug to collect any particles from the blast.

The planned detonation has divided local political figures, with some questioning the safety of the military’s proposal and how the lead azide was allowed to reach such a state.

Others offered support to the US Army. Iowa’s Republican Governor Kim Reynolds, for instance, said the military was taking the right step in going ahead with the detonation.

“I believe, based on the information I’ve been given, that the danger is immediate, and I trust the Army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected,” Reynolds wrote in a social media post on Tuesday.

The controlled detonation is slated to destroy 68 drums containing almost 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I.

The blasts are set to take place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, in the southeastern part of the state.

The facility is a sprawling 7,700-hectare (19,000-acre) installation near Middletown and Des Moines County, about 16 kilometres (10 miles) west of the Mississippi River, which separates Iowa and the state of Illinois.

Environmental groups have raised concerns that the planned explosions would release a cloud of toxic lead into the air, citing a government estimate that the plume could travel more than 160 kilometres (100 miles).

Those particles could eventually land on homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site.

The Iowa Environmental Council and the state branch of the Sierra Club filed a lawsuit on November 19 to stop the detonation, and last week, a federal appeals court issued an administrative stay to pause the planned explosion.

On Monday, President Donald Trump also weighed in, announcing that he had also ordered the military to hold off.

He said that the controlled explosion could proceed only with the agreement of the federal appeals court and Iowa’s Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand.

Later that day, the appeals court lifted its administrative stay, clearing the way for the US Army to proceed with the in-place detonation.

Sand has yet to weigh in on whether he supports the US Army’s plans. He has, however, advocated for greater transparency.

“Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward,” Sand said in a statement on Monday.

“That means they should have the same access to the information I’ve received in briefings from the administration, straight from the source.”

To curb potential lead exposure, federal agencies and the US Army have been rolling out guidance to nearby residents.

In a public safety advisory on Tuesday, the military instructed residents to turn off fans that pull in outside air and switch their heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) systems to a setting that blocks outdoor air intake.

The US Army also advised maximising indoor filtration after the explosion until the lead plume clears.

It is unclear the extent to which the US government will undertake cleanup efforts after the blast.

Under Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) policy, professional cleanup is necessary when as little as five micrograms are present per square foot (0.09 square metres) on floors, or when 40 micrograms are present on the same surface area for windowsills.

Those levels went into effect in January to better protect people — notably young children — from lead exposure.

Lead can cause developmental problems in children, including brain damage and speech problems, and among adults, it can also cause serious harm to internal organs, as well as during pregnancy.

Abatement efforts — designed to reduce lead exposure — are required only when the amount of lead dust meets or exceeds the action levels listed by the EPA.

But Bruce Lanphear, a paediatric epidemiologist and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University, takes issue with the use of regulatory thresholds as a measure of whether to act following the Iowa explosions.

Lead is already ubiquitous in the local environment, owing to decades of industrial activity, historical emissions and other sources, including the lead-based paint commonly used in the 20th century.

A post-detonation reading that falls below an EPA screening threshold would not, by itself, establish that little or no contamination has occurred, according to Lanphear.

“Cleanup should aim to restore lead concentrations to their pre-detonation levels, rather than merely reducing them below a regulatory screening level,” he explained.

“A farmer should not have to accept a substantial increase in soil lead simply because the final concentration remains below a government standard.”

For landowners in the projected fallout area, the detonation may usher in years of federal activity on their property for environmental testing and remediation.

On November 20, the US Army posted a right-of-entry (ROE) form outlining instructions and the terms of that access.

A landowner who signs the form grants the US government and its representatives an irrevocable right to use their property as a work area for up to 36 months.

Federal crews could bring in equipment, erect temporary structures, collect environmental samples, and install groundwater-monitoring wells.

Landowners are under no obligation to sign. But some experts say the agreement offers a means of shifting the burden of environmental monitoring and cleanup to the government.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a public health professor at the University of Iowa, told Al Jazeera that it is not enough for residents to simply hose off outdoor surfaces after the blast.

That might simply wash any lead particles into the surrounding soil, where young children can still ingest it through frequent hand-to-mouth contact.

“You’re just kind of transferring the pollutant from one surface to another,” O’Shaughnessy said.

Even once the lead-dust cloud appears to dissipate, O’Shaughnessy warned that danger could still be present. Lead can remain suspended in air that otherwise looks pristine to the naked eye.

“You can’t just look up in the air and go, ‘Oh, everything looks clear, so I’m fine.’ That’s not going to be the case at all,” O’Shaughnessy explained.

articles.title: A wedding seating row triggered a £400,000 inheritance battle between two brothers after a court found the younger brother and his wife had fraudulently turned their elderly father against the family
articles.summary: A family wedding seating dispute has sparked a £400,000 inheritance battle between two brothers after a court found that a younger son and his wife had
articles.body: A family wedding seating dispute has sparked a £400,000 inheritance battle between two brothers after a court found that a younger son and his wife had fraudulently influenced their elderly father to change his will. The row, which began more than 30 years ago and escalated at a wedding in 2011, ended with the court overturning a will that left the entire estate to the couple. Instead, the judge reinstated an earlier will dividing the inheritance among four branches of the family. The judge also ordered the younger brother to pay £115,000 towards his older brother's legal costs.£5,000 loan and wedding seating row fuel brothers' bitter feudThe disagreement between the brothers dated back more than 30 years, with tensions reportedly developing over a dispute involving missing stock at a grocery shop previously run by Bani. Another source of resentment was a £5,000 loan that Bani had given Harish to help him establish the DJ career he wanted to pursue. The money was reportedly never repaid, according to the account presented during the trial.The hostility between the siblings intensified at the wedding of Bani's eldest daughter in 2011. Harish and his wife attended a family gathering following the wedding but were unable to find seats. According to the judge, they attempted to sit in available places but were told by another family member, rather than Bani, that the seats had been reserved. Harish interpreted the situation as an indication that he was unwelcome and left the gathering, while Bani regarded his departure as a hostile gesture in front of both families.Brothers' family feud worsens after heated confrontation at father's homeThe judge noted that the incident had a lasting impact on their relationship. Bani believed Harish had walked out of the celebration, while Harish felt he had not been made welcome. Their disagreement continued in a later confrontation at Harish's home, where their father was staying. The brothers gave different accounts of the incident, with Bani claiming he had been thrown out and Harish saying he had told his older brother to leave.Recorder Cohen said the consequences made it more difficult for Bani to visit his father at Harish's home, although Gowerdhan's own property was less than 100 yards away. The judge also noted that Harish acknowledged during cross-examination that he did not like his brother and actually hated him.Father cuts older son out of will three months before his deathGowerdhan had previously made a will in 2015 that divided his estate among his two surviving sons and the families of his two other children, who had died. However, in November 2023, approximately three months before his death, he made a new will leaving his entire estate, including his home in Northmead Road, Slough, to Harish and Paramjit. The change excluded Bani and the rest of the family from receiving any inheritance.The new arrangement prompted Bani to take legal action, alleging that his younger brother had unduly influenced their father and turned him against other relatives. The later will also contained a specific explanation for excluding Bani, stating that there had been little or no contact between them for years and that Bani was financially independent. Harish maintained that his older brother had become distant from their father during his final years.Harish's barrister, Nina Roberts, argued that her client and his wife had become the central figures in Gowerdhan's life. She said they had cared for the pensioner, visited him regularly and helped him maintain as much independence as possible. She also argued that Bani had played no part in his father's life when the final will was made.Harish further maintained that he believed Bani had lost contact with their father. When Gowerdhan made similar statements about having little contact with other members of his immediate family in front of the solicitor preparing the will, Harish said he did not consider it his responsibility to correct him. He also raised questions about Bani's behaviour at their father's funeral, pointing to his decision to wear a Scottish Tam-o'-Shanter bonnet and his conduct during the occasion.Brother and wife accused of misleading father to secure £400,000 estateAfter hearing the evidence, Recorder Cohen found that Harish and Paramjit had influenced Gowerdhan by making him believe that other family members were no longer interested in maintaining contact with him. The judge accepted that the couple had provided loving care during the pensioner's final years but concluded that Gowerdhan had become increasingly vulnerable as he grew older.The judge said Harish had made false representations to his father to persuade him to change his will, knowing that the statements were untrue. He also highlighted that Harish had been present when Gowerdhan told the solicitor that he no longer had contact with his immediate family apart from Harish and Paramjit. According to the judge, Harish knew this impression was false but did nothing to correct it.Recorder Cohen described the false statements as particularly significant because some family members had made considerable efforts to remain in contact with Gowerdhan. He concluded that Harish and Paramjit had poisoned the pensioner's mind for their own financial benefit, ruling that their actions amounted to fraudulent calumny.The judge also found that Paramjit had contributed to the situation by keeping Gowerdhan away from his other daughter-in-law, Harjinder, after the later will was made. Neither Harish nor Paramjit had informed the wider family about plans to sell Gowerdhan's property, combine some of the proceeds and purchase a house together. The court ultimately concluded that the later will had been brought about by the couple's fraudulent actions and could not stand.Court restores £400,000 inheritance split and orders brother to pay £115,000Following the ruling, the later will was overturned, and Gowerdhan's 2015 will was reinstated. Under that arrangement, the £400,000 estate was divided into four shares between Bani, Harish and the families of their two deceased siblings. Each branch of the family was entitled to approximately £100,000 under the earlier inheritance arrangement.However, the ruling also brought a significant financial consequence for Harish and Paramjit. The judge ordered the couple to pay the costs of the legal dispute, including an initial payment of £115,000 towards Bani's legal fees, pending a full assessment of the bills. They were also ordered to cover their own substantial legal costs incurred during the proceedings.The costs order effectively wiped out Harish's share of the inheritance, despite the reinstatement of the will that entitled him to a portion of the estate. The decision therefore meant that Bani's challenge resulted in the restoration of the original four-way inheritance arrangement, while his younger brother faced a substantial financial liability arising from the court proceedings.The case followed a week-long trial at Central London County Court, where the judge considered the brothers' longstanding disagreements, the circumstances surrounding the changes to Gowerdhan's will and the evidence about the family's contact with the pensioner. The court's ruling established that the later inheritance arrangement had been secured through fraudulent calumny and reinstated the distribution set out in the 2015 will.Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly available, including court proceedings and the judgment concerning the inheritance dispute involving Gowerdhan Dass and his family. The details of the family dispute, alleged fraudulent influence, inheritance arrangements and legal costs have been reported based on the court's findings. articles.title: An Ohio couple divorced in 2015 but kept a Colorado house in a family trust; when the husband stopped paying its expenses, his ex-wife covered them, and an appeals court recalculated his share at $101,723
articles.summary: A divorce settlement can leave former spouses financially connected long after their marriage ends.
articles.body: A divorce settlement can leave former spouses financially connected long after their marriage ends. In Ohio, a couple who divorced in 2015 continued to share responsibility for a Colorado property held in an irrevocable family trust. Years later, a dispute over unpaid taxes, insurance, utilities and maintenance expenses led to a court battle after the former wife began paying the bills herself.In a November 20, 2026, decision in Sturt v. Sturt, available on Justia, the Ohio Court of Appeals, Sixth District, reversed a lower court ruling that had removed several maintenance expenses from the former husband's obligations. The appellate court calculated that he owed his former wife $101,723.27 for expenses she had covered.Divorce agreement placed property expenses on husbandDiane E Sturt and Willard H Sturt married on June 12, 1993, and divorced on January 6, 2015. Their divorce judgment addressed a property in Minturn, Colorado, which was to be held in an irrevocable trust for their benefit, with their two daughters receiving the property through a right of survivorship. Both former spouses were designated as co-trustees.Under the divorce judgment, Willard was responsible for all expenses connected with the property, including mortgage payments, real estate taxes, utilities and maintenance. Diane was required to reimburse him annually for either half of the actual expenses or $5,000, whichever was less, after he provided the relevant bills and payment records. The agreement also required both parties to share the cost of property insurance equally, with Diane initially purchasing the insurance and Willard reimbursing half.Former wife paid bills after husband stopped paymentsDiane filed a motion asking the court to hold Willard in contempt on September 19, 2023. She alleged that he had stopped paying the property's expenses in late 2020, leaving her to cover insurance premiums, property taxes, water bills, internet service and necessary repairs. She testified that she had tried contacting him through letters and his workplace but received little response. Some utility services were at risk of being disconnected, while maintenance problems continued to develop.During an October 1, 2024, hearing, Diane presented invoices and payment records. Her expenses included $15,843 in homeowners' insurance, $18,446.61 in property taxes, $3,560.34 in water bills and maintenance work involving the roof, exterior, deck, plumbing and heating systems. Willard acknowledged that he had stopped paying the property's expenses and had not paid property taxes or insurance since 2020. He also admitted that several repairs were necessary but argued that Diane had hired contractors without obtaining his consent. He maintained that he wanted to choose the workers or perform some repairs himself.Lower court removed maintenance expenses from orderThe magistrate found Willard in contempt and calculated that he owed Diane $40,171.50, including his share of taxes, insurance, utilities and maintenance. It also ordered $5,000 in attorney fees and $150 in costs.However, in September 2025, the Lucas County Court of Common Pleas modified the decision. It concluded that Diane could not independently arrange maintenance work and demand reimbursement without first obtaining Willard's approval. It removed the maintenance expenses from the contempt finding and cancelled the attorney fee and cost awards. The court retained the contempt finding concerning unpaid taxes, insurance and utilities.Appeals court reverses ruling and recalculates reimbursementDiane challenged the decision on five grounds, arguing that Willard had failed to fulfil his obligations and that the lower court had improperly changed the divorce agreement. The Sixth District agreed that the original judgment clearly made Willard responsible for all expenses connected with the Colorado property. It found that he had deliberately ignored those obligations despite knowing that repairs and payments were necessary.The judges also ruled that the divorce agreement did not require Willard's consent before Diane could arrange necessary maintenance. Requiring her to obtain his approval would effectively modify the original agreement. After reviewing the payment records, the appellate court recalculated the expenses. It included $48,821 for exterior log restoration, $13,911 for deck and railing work, $5,000 for roof repairs, $8,200 for heat tape installation, $1,800 for shower repairs, $163.23 for sealant and $2,144 for a refrigerator replacement. It also recognised $1,300 for sprinkler maintenance, which had already been allowed by the magistrate.The court calculated Willard's total outstanding obligation at $101,723.27, rejecting Diane's higher calculation of $103,654.89. The appellate court reversed the September 23, 2025, judgment and ordered Willard to pay the costs of the appeal. It also sent the attorney fee issue back to the lower court to reconsider the relevant equitable factors and decide whether a hearing was warranted.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: "The View" co-host Sunny Hostin said Tuesday that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has "never been wrong about anything," pointing to her reaction to the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and President Donald Trump's role. Hostin read the former Secretary of State's post to X, which said, "Is it a national security scandal? Yes. Is it a corruption scandal? Yes. Is it an insider trading scandal? Yes. Is it a market manipulation scandal? Yes. If it’s 'super intelligence,' call it Supergate." "She's never been wrong, and this is just what it is," she added. Hostin claimed Trump made "approximately $15 million" upon Huang being reinstated through the company's stock rise. A Financial Times report said the president could have made up to $15 million upon Huang's return. TRUMP ACCUSED OF 'SOCIALISM, COMMUNISM' AFTER HELPING SCANDAL-PLAGUED NVIDIA CEO RECLAIM TOP JOB "The board is not doing its job — the board of this company — and what the board asked the government, which shouldn't even be a conversation, they asked the government whether or not the Trump administration would make sure or would qualify that Jensen was not a national security risk," Hostin said. "Trump said he's not a national security risk, which is not true. And then second, they asked that the Justice Department not be investigating him… This is corruption to the highest level." MS NOW HOST THREATENS TO EJECT ‘TECH BRO’ GUEST DURING JENSEN HUANG DEBATE, WARNS 'THE DOOR'S RIGHT THERE!' "Sunny Hostin is an extremely unlikeable, talentless hack with a poorly rated TV show who clearly suffers from a severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome. I lose brain cells every single time I have the displeasure of hearing her speak," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital. Clinton has appeared on "The View" numerous times over the years, with friendly receptions on the liberal-leaning show. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Nvidia's board decided to bring back Huang after he resigned earlier this month following reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly identified as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Trump spoke with CNBC on Monday after Huang was reinstated, revealing that he intervened to get him back on as CEO. JENSEN HUANG IS BACK. NVIDIA’S BOARD STILL OWES AMERICA ANSWERS "Yeah, the answer is no," Trump told CNBC in an interview when asked about the development and whether Huang could have been reinstated without his input. "I believe my intervention was very important."
