articles.title: Libya’s Haftar visits Turkiye days after Ukraine hits Russian warship
articles.summary: Ahead of Erdogan’s Libya trip, Haftar’s visit suggests Turkiye seeks another way to bring the country’s rivals together.
articles.body:
Eastern Libyan military commander Khalifa Haftar, flanked by his sons, arrived in Ankara on his first known visit to Turkiye, just days after a long-range Ukrainian attack struck a Russian ship in Benghazi.

Arriving on Tuesday to the Turkish capital, the Libyan commander was greeted by Turkish Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu at the airport, according to photos released by the General Command of the Libyan National Army (LNA).

There was no official media readout of the meeting, but Reuters news agency reported that Haftar is set to meet with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Khaled and Belqasim Haftar accompanied their father to Ankara, according to the LNA’s General Command. Khaled is the LNA’s chief of staff, and Belqasim heads Libya’s Development and Reconstruction Fund.

Saddam Haftar, the LNA’s deputy commander and heir apparent, was in Doha for a separate meeting with Qatar’s minister of state for defence.

The visit came two days after Ukraine struck a Russian warship in Benghazi, the main city in Haftar-controlled eastern Libya, killing at least 10 Libyan and Russian crew members, according to local authorities.

The warship had docked to refuel and resupply under an agreement with the eastern authorities. Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli condemned the attack on Monday, saying neither Russia nor Ukraine had the right to conduct military operations on Libyan territory or in its waters.

However, Turkish military support predates Ukraine’s long-range attack as Ankara helped the then-Tripoli government repel Haftar’s forces’ offensive in 2019 and 2020. Since a United Nations-brokered ceasefire ended major fighting in 2020, Turkiye has built ties with Haftar’s camp while maintaining its alliance with Tripoli.

On Saturday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, prime minister of Libya’s Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, in Istanbul. Fidan later gave an interview to a Turkish television station, revealing Erdogan will visit Libya in December after a 15-year hiatus.

Khalifa Haftar’s visit to Ankara comes just weeks after Libya’s eastern-based House of Representatives approved a 2019 maritime deal with Turkiye, reversing years of opposition, largely seen as an overture towards Turkiye as power-sharing talks in the country stall.

Khalifa Haftar’s son Saddam Haftar is reportedly eyeing the Libyan presidency role, backed by Washington.

Championed by Massad Boulos, United States President Donald Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, the US is currently trying to broker a power-sharing proposal between Tripoli and Benghazi that would make Saddam Haftar the chairman of the Tripoli-based Presidency Council (PC).

Powerful factions in Tripoli and the western city of Misrata oppose giving Saddam the post, Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“The Turks are more pragmatic and realistic than Boulos,” Harchaoui said. Ankara takes that opposition seriously, he said, because trying to force the appointment could destabilise Libya.

As Haftar pushes for the president role, approving the 2019 memorandum of understanding signed between Turkiye and Libya’s UN-recognised former Government of National Accord (GNA) on the delimitation of maritime boundaries between the two countries in the Mediterranean Sea was an effort to secure Ankara’s backing for the council chairmanship position, Harchaoui said.

The European Union condemned the vote, as did Greece, Israel and Egypt.

Despite Saddam Haftar’s absence from the Ankara meeting, by inviting his father, Harchaoui said, Erdogan has given himself another way to show progress in bringing Libya’s rivals together.

As Erdogan gears up for a visit to Libya, the Turkish president may seek a meeting between Dbeibah and Khalifa Haftar as Ankara’s effort to carve “a format of its own, calibrated to its own risk appetite and independent of the one Boulos has been pushing for months”, according to the analyst.

articles.title: 3 Chinese satellites scanned India’s western coast frequently during Op Sindoor: Desi space surveillance company’s report
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Three Chinese surveillance satellites hovered over India’s western coast, especially over Gujarat, during the entire duration of Operation
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Three Chinese surveillance satellites hovered over India’s western coast, especially over Gujarat, during the entire duration of Operation Sindoor last year, a report by Indian space surveillance and intelligence company Digantara revealed.Apart from keeping an eye on India’s naval and air force bases in the Indian Ocean Region, the three satellites — Ningxia-14, Gaofen-11 and Yaogan-30 — monitored critical commercial infrastructure and ports, including Reliance’s Jamnagar refinery, and especially areas around Bhuj, Naliya and Jamnagar during the Indo-Pak conflict, some of the report findings shared by Digantara with TOI said.While Bhuj Rudra Mata Air Force Station is a key airbase in Kachchh near the Pakistan border, Naliya is important as it hosts an air force station (49th wing) in western Kachchh, a forward base near the Pakistan border and Arabian Sea. Its proximity to both land and maritime approaches enables rapid air defence, surveillance, and operational response across India’s western frontier.All of these Chinese satellites, especially Yaogan-43 01G, which are equipped with high-resolution visual imaging and electronic intelligence gathering capabilities, altered their orbital parameters on May 7, 2025, the day Op Sindoor began — the conflict lasted four days. This altered manoeuvre extended their observation windows over Indian military installations, the report found.It was also noted in the report that the Chinese satellites made frequent and unusual manoeuvres to focus on the Pahalgam area in the days before the terror attack on April 22 last year.From the military’s point of view, the western coast of India is important as it’s a vital hub for the Indian Navy. Headquartered in Mumbai under the Western Naval Command, this coastline anchors India’s maritime security and power projection in the western Indian Ocean. Major hubs like Mumbai, Goa and Karwar support surface combatants, submarines, naval aviation and ship construction. The Western Naval Command guards critical energy and trade routes in the Arabian Sea.The western coast is also significant commercially due to its natural harbours, busy seaports, energy infrastructure and marine resources. Stretching across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Kerala, it supports high-volume trade with West Asia, Africa and Europe.

articles.title: Chinese tech giant Huawei convicted of federal charges, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets
articles.summary: Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York on Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens.
articles.body: Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York on Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens. A jury in New York’s Eastern District found the company and three of its subsidiaries guilty of seven conspiracy counts that included bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, defrauding the United States and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. In the roughly two-month trial, Huawei was also convicted of bank fraud and wire fraud. Huawei was acquitted of two counts, a racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice. “For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception,” Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva said in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.” In a statement, Huawei said the charges are “without legal or factual merit,” and it said it welcomes the racketeering verdict. “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” the company said. Huawei attorney Brian Heberling said the company plans to appeal. At sentencing, which is scheduled for Sept. 14, Huawei could face fines, forfeiture and restitution. Prosecutors accused the company, which makes smartphones and has telecom networks around the world, of encouraging its workforce of 200,000 in 170 countries to lie, cheat, and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.” Huawei was accused of misappropriating intellectual property like source code, user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology and robot testing technology, prosecutors said. T-Mobile, Cisco, Quintel and CNEX were among the companies whose technology was stolen, federal prosecutors said in a news release Tuesday. In Iran, the company assisted the regime with “turnkey” internet services and mobile networks, prosecutors said, and it provided surveillance cameras that allowed officials to monitor protests. Huawei also helped intelligence agents monitor and censor the internet, prosecutors said. Huawei then lied to banks about the nature of its business in Iran, allowing the company to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and become what prosecutors described as “a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services.” In an interview Tuesday, Heberling rejected the government’s allegations, saying prosecutors presented a “caricature-like portrait” of Huawei of as a corrupt organization with company policies that condoned crime. “That was just profoundly inconsistent with the company that I experienced in my work, but more importantly, [with] the evidence, which really showed a series of isolated events over a 20-year period,” he said. “No company can insure perfection over that period of time.” Heberling argued that the racketeering acquittal — the most serious charge the company faced — showed a “profound rejection of the narrative the United States pursued in this case.” Huawei was previously banned from selling equipment to U.S. carriers over fears that it poses a security risk, according to the Associated Press, and it was blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.

articles.title: From ghat to gallery, Banaras set for brush with art
articles.summary: To linger in Banaras is to linger in another era, an era which one cannot quite date by century,\" wrote Harvard scholar Diana L Eck in 'Banaras: City of
articles.body: To linger in Banaras is to linger in another era, an era which one cannot quite date by century," wrote Harvard scholar Diana L Eck in 'Banaras: City of Light'. The inaugural CII Banaras Biennale, which opens on Nov 27 and is on view till Dec 31, gives art lovers a new excuse to linger in one of India's oldest cities.Despite its noisy, crowded lanes and walls with their own artwork of paan stains, the city is more than the Instagram reels of Ganga aarti and sunset boat rides suggest. Aptly themed 'Kashi/Light; City as Sensorium', the biennale seeks to put Banaras on the cultural map, but without treating it as a mere backdrop. "The biennale is envisioned as a long-term commitment to positioning Banaras as a global capital of living culture," says Madhav Singhania, chairman of the steering committee of CII Banaras Biennale 2026. The Biennale spans visual art, textiles, craft, music, performance and scholarship, with events spread across ghats and galleries.That approach is rooted in the idea that the city's past and present need not be kept apart. At the centre of the exhibition is Bharatiya Kala Bhavan (BKB) inside the Banaras Hindu University campus, where lead curator Gayatri Sinha has chosen to place contemporary work among the museum's extensive collection of more than one lakh objects. "Can we make the ancient and the contemporary conversational?" she asks.The question is the aesthetic thread that ties the biennale together. There is a more literal dhaga, too - of silk and zari. Pramod Kumar KG, who is curating the textile and craft section, is looking to connect Banaras's mastery of the loom with contemporary fashion and design.BKB's collection began with art historian Rai Krishna Das, who started collecting in 1920. Its present building was inaugurated by Jawaharlal Nehru in 1962. The main gallery houses Sinha's exhibition, 'The Cycle of Life: Samsara', which looks at life, death, livelihood and renunciation in Banaras. "If you visit Varanasi, sooner or later, this integration between life and death, between life, livelihood and renunciation, between the appropriation of a certain sensibility and the letting go of your human education becomes very important."Sinha draws from BKB's impressive collection of terracotta sculptures, miniature paintings, textiles and coins, and makes connections with contemporary art. Terracotta heads, some nearly 2,000 years old, are shown alongside a contemporary work in the medium by Ravinder Reddy. Manu Parekh, whose artistic practice has repeatedly returned to Banaras, also features in the exhibition. An 11ft-by-11ft tapestry based on his work, woven by Karishma Swali's Chanakya School of Craft, evokes the city at night.Biennales in India have usually been led by artists, curators or foundations, but this one brings industry and cultural institutions such as the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art and Sunil Munjal's Serendipity Arts together. "This is sort of curatorially led, but industry-driven," says Tarana Sawhney, chairperson of the CII Art & Culture Committee.The intention is not simply to parachute a festival into the city and leave. "We didn't want to create a festival that just went in, kind of engaged with the city and left," Sawhney says. Skilling and textile development initiatives are part of a larger effort that will continue after visitors have gone. For Sinha, the work is ultimately about bringing objects, histories and artistic practices together without erasing their differences. In Banaras, where the old and the everyday share the same streets, that conversation is already part of the city.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Colombian president blames ex-FARC rebels for car bomb blast
articles.summary: Colombian President De la Espriella blames the FARC for plotting a bombing that injured tens and pledges to retaliate.
articles.body:
Bogota, Colombia – Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has blamed ex-FARC rebels for a car bomb attack last night targeting a state government building, which injured at least 23 people.

On a visit to Villavicencio on Tuesday, where the attack took place, the president accused Antonio Medina, a commander of the Central General Staff (EMC) rebel group, of plotting the bombing in retaliation for government offensives in the province.

“The bandit Antonio Medina from the [FARC] dissidents is to blame, and we’re going to go after him and make him pay with blood,” de la Espriella told reporters.

Last night’s attack rocked the seat of government in Meta, a province bordering the capital, Bogota, to the southeast. Videos show extensive damage to the building in Villavicencio, which houses the governor’s office, as well as surrounding businesses and vehicles.

The Head of National Police Operations, Ricardo Alarcon, told local media that initial tests indicate the car was laden with between 80 and 100kg (176-220 pounds) of pentolite, a high explosive used in military warheads, as well as civilian mining.

Meta was a historical heartland for the FARC, which officially demobilised following a historic peace deal in 2016. In the years since, dissident rebels who refused to lay down their arms or returned to war have expanded their control in the province, a key access point to the coca plantations, gold mining and drug smuggling routes of the Amazon River Basin.

The most powerful group is the EMC, headed by alias Ivan Mordisco, one of Colombia’s most wanted men. The government earlier this year announced a bounty of 5 billion pesos (roughly $1.4m) for his capture or killing.

In recent months, the government has increased pressure on the EMC, bombing its camps and targeting senior members. Just yesterday, the president confirmed the killing of alias El Churco, an EMC commander.

The campaign is part of the new far-right government’s security pivot, which aims to tackle criminal organisations through military force and has suspended the negotiations initiated under the previous government.

De la Espriella has suggested that last night’s bombing in Villavicencio was likely a retaliation against ramped-up state pressure on armed groups.

“The narco-terrorists are running wild, launching desperate attacks, because they know we are defeating them and that their end is near,” the president wrote on X this morning.

The attack, which happened on the eve of the 10-year anniversary of the 2016 peace deal, highlights the growing risks to civilians under de la Espriella’s heavy-handed security strategy, say experts.

“As the government increases pressure, armed and criminal groups are trying to raise the cost of doing that for the government by exerting pain, instilling fear and causing direct harm against communities and against the civilian population,” said Elizabeth Dickinson, deputy director for Latin America at the International Crisis Group.

articles.title: FAA issues ground delay at Chicago O'Hare due to 'equipment outage'
articles.summary: An equipment outage prompted the FAA to issue a Tuesday afternoon ground stop at Chicago O'Hare International Airport, delaying flights until at least 4:15 p.m.
articles.body: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop Tuesday at Chicago O'Hare International Airport due to an "equipment outage," during what is anticipated to be a heavy Thanksgiving travel rush before changing it to a brief ground delay. The FAA reported the ground stop just after 3 p.m. local time Tuesday. The ground stop was expected to be lifted by 4:15 p.m., according to local reports. The ground delay was canceled around 5 p.m. local time. "Due to EQUIPMENT / OUTAGE, departure traffic destined to Chicago OHare International Airport, Chicago, IL (ORD) is currently experiencing delays averaging 47 minutes," the FAA website states. TRAVELERS CLASH OVER WHETHER CRUISE LINES SHOULD ALLOW DOGS AND CATS ON BOARD OR NOT The FAA identified the issue as an outage involving equipment used to track aircraft and vehicles on the airport surface, Fox 32 reported. "The FAA is no longer under a ground stop at Chicago O’Hare International Airport but is temporarily delaying some flights while technicians work to repair a piece of air traffic equipment," the agency said. The agency did not say what caused the outage. The issue was limited to O’Hare, and it does not impact all flights nor affect any other airports or FAA systems, the FAA said. The initial advisory listed a delay of up to 42 minutes for flights covered by the ground stop, Fox 32 reported. In a separate status update, the FAA reported arrival delays of 15 minutes or less for flights already in the air. The advisory did not specify what equipment was affected. Tuesday’s ground stop followed a separate one at the same airport on Monday morning because of staffing issues. Flight delays and cancellations have been at the forefront of the minds of travelers, given what happened on Nov. 13, when every plane was grounded as part of a massive nationwide ground stop. articles.title: A question of trust in the NHS could be Swinney's most dangerous political moment
articles.summary: The Scottish government has to convince the public and political rivals that it has a grip on the problems at NHS Grampian.
articles.body:
At its heart this is a story about trust.

Trust in doctors and other health professionals at NHS Grampian to provide the highest standards of treatment and care.

Trust in their managers to effectively deal with problems when they arise.

And trust in the Scottish government to step in if that does not happen.

What we have learned about the operation of NHS Grampian in the last two weeks raises huge questions in all of these areas.

First we had a scathing report by the watchdog Healthcare Improvement Scotland, which found serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian's leadership and oversight of clinical governance.

There was particular concern about patterns of repeated and avoidable harm, and the board's ability to learn from serious adverse events.

Does Scotland's NHS have a revolving door problem with senior managers?

Surgeon calls for corporate homicide probe over claims patients unnecessarily bled to death

Man who nearly died during liver surgery at Aberdeen hospital says mistakes were made

The Scottish government has sent in a support team to help the current management at NHS Grampian make improvements.

Questions have been raised about the suitability of some of those appointed to carry out this work given problems they have faced in their own areas of responsibility .

The watchdog's report was followed by a powerful intervention from a surgeon-turned-whistleblower who works at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

Dr Mohammed Habib said he had been raising serious concerns about liver and pancreatic services at the hospital for 10 years.

He released a previously unpublished review from 2022 that looked at 45 patients in the care of this specialist unit over the previous seven years.

It said that 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention.

Nineteen people died and their deaths were potentially avoidable.

This finding was not made public by NHS Grampian or those in the Scottish government who knew about it.

This is where this story becomes political - because Dr Habib tried to get the attention of ministers.

He raised his concerns with the Scottish government including, he said, writing to the first minister on three occasions.

At Holyrood question time, John Swinney acknowledged that the issues raised were of the "gravest concern".

He said Dr Habib's messages had received "appropriate responses" from officials.

It seems they directed him to a national whistleblowing service and to the police.

This is what, in my view, makes this potentially the most dangerous political moment for John Swinney since he took over as first minister in 2024.

A surgeon writes to him because 19 people may have died unnecessarily as a result of how they were treated by the NHS and nothing seems to happen.

We have since been told that Swinney's office did not make him personally aware of this correspondence.

That in turn raises questions about the operation of the highest political office in devolved Scotland.

After two decades in power would the SNP administration not have an established system for deciding what should and should not be seen by the first minister?

And if a pattern of seemingly avoidable deaths in the NHS is not serious enough to be escalated to the top then what is?

Swinney seemed to recognise the inadequacy of his parliamentary answers fairly quickly.

Soon after question time his team said he had asked the Scottish government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handled.

This too was only the beginning of a realisation within government that this had the potential to develop into a political disaster.

By Saturday, Health Secretary Angela Constance had decided to announce an independent review into who knew what and when, what they did with the information - and why.

Before the weekend was out, she was on BBC Scotland's The Sunday Show promising 100% transparency and accountability.

She seemed angry to have been left carrying the can for something that should have been dealt with more robustly at a far earlier stage.

We have now learned that the review will be led by an experienced King's Counsel , and the likelihood is that they will come from outside Scotland.

Constance has said that any clinical input they receive will definitely come from outside Scotland.

The KC will be able to scrutinise the actions of current and former ministers, civil servants, and those working in the health service.

Constance said their findings would be published in full and that any urgent matters that arise during the review should be reported directly to relevant bodies.

The minister also said it was "categorically false" to say that no action was taken following the 2022 report, which was drawn up by University of Edinburgh Professor Stephen Wigmore.

Constance said liver and pancreatic surgery was suspended for a time, then resumed under the professor's supervision until he was satisfied it could continue without his oversight.

It was stopped again on at least two further occasions and patients requiring complex surgery have been transferred to NHS Lothian since early this year.

It has been reported that former Health Secretary Humza Yousaf and current chief medical officer Sir Gregor Smith were aware of the 2022 review.

Yousaf has made clear he supports full scrutiny and "further dramatic action" in NHS Grampian. Sir Gregor has yet to make any public comment.

The review process will not necessarily contain this crisis of confidence.

More patients and their families may come forward to share their experiences, or perhaps others within NHS Grampian will choose to speak out.

The involvement of the campaigning lawyer Aamer Anwar, who is working with Dr Habib, increases the likelihood of this type of follow-up.

There will undoubtedly be further parliamentary scrutiny, with the possibility of key figures being called before a Holyrood committee.

It is worth remembering that the police are also taking an interest and have yet to determine whether or not a formal investigation is merited.

Some have hinted at the potential need for a judge-led public inquiry, although these tend to take a very long time and cost a huge amount of money.

There are already three health-related public inquiries into Covid handling, major hospital building projects in Glasgow and Edinburgh, and botched brain surgery in Dundee.

There is a clear determination by government and opposition at Holyrood to see a much faster remedy to the complexity of problems in NHS Grampian.

A turnaround in healthcare delivery and management in north east Scotland is being pursued alongside radical plans to overhaul how the NHS is run across the country.

The government is proposing to merge the existing network of regional health boards into just two for the whole of mainland Scotland.

There will be those who argue that this provides an opportunity to create a more robust system of supervision and a more rapid response when things go wrong.

Others fear that this kind of centralisation could result in local deficiencies being overlooked.

This could become an important feature in the debate over NHS reform.

In the meantime, the Scottish government has to convince the public and political rivals that it has got a grip of what's happening in NHS Grampian.

That seems essential if patients are to have confidence that they can place their trust in the vital services it provides.

articles.title: Is Black Friday even Black Friday anymore? Here’s how (and why) the busiest shopping day of the year transformed over time
articles.summary: Experts chart the history of Black Friday, how it got its name and why it changed over the years. Plus, 2026 predictions for sales and bestselling products.
articles.body: Lines wrapped around department stores, fights over products and crowds so large they poured out of retailers’ front doors used to be par for the course on Black Friday. But in recent years, what defines the shopping event has significantly changed. There’s no more sprinting into stores before sunrise to snag 24-hour doorbusters — now, Black Friday competes with Cyber Monday, causing most sales to shift online, start earlier and stick around longer. Some even say that Black Friday has transformed into Black November, a term experts use to describe the month-long discounts leading up to Thanksgiving weekend. To help you understand what Black Friday is exactly, and how it’s become the busiest shopping day in the U.S., I spoke to experts about its history and charted how it’s changed since its inception. Experts also shared their predictions for Black Friday 2026 — spoiler alert: it’s likely going to be another record-breaking year even though consumers are feeling major economic pressure. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What is Black Friday? Black Friday, which happens the day after Thanksgiving, is one of the biggest shopping events of the year in the U.S. Every retailer you can think of offers major deals online and/or in stores, and many of them sell products at their lowest prices in months, if not all year or ever. Black Friday started in the U.S. and Americans associate it with Thanksgiving, but it’s gone global. Over 20 countries, including the United Kingdom, Italy, Sweden and Mexico, host similar events, and some even call it “Black Friday.” The shopping extravaganza also happens simultaneously worldwide, despite other countries not celebrating their version of Thanksgiving (or, in some cases, any version of Thanksgiving) within the November timeframe. For example, retailers in Canada host Black Friday sales on the same day as those in the U.S., but the country recognizes the second Monday in October as its Thanksgiving holiday. When is Black Friday? Black Friday is technically the day after Thanksgiving, which is November 27, 2026. But recently, retailers have started their sales earlier, changing the sale from a 24-hour shopping sprint to a month-long savings marathon. That said, Black Friday stopped being a one-day shopping event well before early deals made it obvious. Retailers originally competed to see who could open first on Black Friday, and eventually, some welcomed shoppers into stores on Thanksgiving, transforming the sale into a five-day shopping weekend: It began on Thanksgiving and ended on Cyber Monday. Then, because so much shopping during that period was happening online, experts named it the Cyber Five. Those five days expanded into a week, then multiple weeks, then a whole month, leading experts to dub all of November “Black November.” Why do Black Friday sales start so early? Black Friday sales starting so early is evidence that retailers are responding to modern consumer behavior trends. People want ample time to shop across multiple weeks, helping them avoid “lumpy spending,” or concentrated purchases during the holidays with subsequent massive bills, says Dr. Ross Steinman, a professor of consumer psychology at Widener University. Retailers noticed a strong increase in this type of early holiday shopping and adjusted their sales schedules accordingly. In 2022, Amazon even created an additional sale to kick off early holiday shopping: Prime Big Deal Days, which is essentially a second Prime Day. The annual Prime member-exclusive event happens in early October, and to remain competitive, other retailers like Target, Walmart and Best Buy started running corresponding sales. Once they’re over, it’s time for early Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals to roll out. Despite a now prolonged period of early deals, sales on Black Friday itself haven’t softened… for the most part. In 2021, revenue growth reversed year over year for the first time: Black Friday sales totaled $8.9 billion, compared to $9 billion in 2020, according to Adobe. But that hasn’t happened since. In fact, sales have steadily increased, and in 2026, Adobe forecasts that consumers will spend $12.9 billion during Black Friday, up 9.2% year over year. What has softened, however, is the number of consumers shopping during Thanksgiving weekend: the National Retail Federation projects that there will be 182.7 million potential shoppers during that timeframe in 2026, down slightly from 186.9 million in 2025. The cause of the dip? Early shopping. More and more, shoppers are taking advantage of deals as they pop up instead of waiting until the end of November. Experts say that Thanksgiving weekend will remain the busiest and biggest shopping period of the year, but turnout isn’t likely to exponentially increase anymore. How has online shopping impacted Black Friday? Online shopping has dramatically impacted Black Friday, an event that originated as an in-person, social shopping experience. During its inception, it was purposely timed to happen the Friday after Thanksgiving, a paid holiday for most employees who were home and looking for something to do — retailers started slashing prices on merchandise to draw shoppers into stores with their friends and family. The first major sign that Black Friday’s identity was changing from a predominantly in-store experience to an e-commerce one happened in 2019: For the first time, Black Friday topped Cyber Monday as the busiest day for online shopping, according to the NRF. Then, in 2020, the Covid-19 pandemic further motivated retailers to reinvent their typical Black Friday offerings by promoting online shopping and transforming days-long sales into months-long savings events. These efforts worked in retailers’ favor: the number of online Black Friday shoppers surpassed a record 100 million in 2020, according to the NRF. Retailers have approached Black Friday with similar strategies ever since, resulting in comparable trends for the past six years. Every year since 2019, there’s been more total online shoppers during Black Friday than during Cyber Monday, according to the NRF. However, people historically spend more on Cyber Monday than on Black Friday, according to Adobe. This may be due to messaging on retailers’ websites indicating that Cyber Monday is shoppers’ last chance to take advantage of deals, says Steinman. Some websites even have clocks counting the seconds until Cyber Monday is over. By creating pressure to check out before midnight, retailers add a gamification element to their sales, making shoppers more competitive while deal-hunting, says Steinman. So, does all this mean that in-person shopping on Black Friday is dead? No, but it no longer defines the holiday. Black Friday is still the most popular day for in-store shopping over the Thanksgiving weekend, with 85.7 million people participating during Black Friday 2025, according to the NRF. The main segment of shoppers who visit stores in person on Black Friday are those steeped in tradition, says Steinman. They see Black Friday from an experiential lens — they want to spend time with loved ones while browsing deals and are reluctant to give up that yearly outing together. How much does the average shopper spend on Black Friday? In 2025, the average shopper spent $337.86 during the Thanksgiving weekend (from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday), according to the NRF. That marked an increase from 2024’s average spend of $315.56. In 2026, experts don’t foresee shoppers spending less despite feeling their budgets squeezed by high inflation rates and months of soaring fuel prices. “What’s striking is that economic instability has not caused consumers to stop spending; rather, it has made them more strategic,” says Claudia Townsend, a consumer behavior researcher and marketing professor at the University of Miami. People are hungrier than ever for savings, both on holiday-related purchases like gifts and decor, and everyday basics to ease the burden of rebuying things they constantly run out of. They’re taking their time to find the best deals possible so they can buy what’s on their wish lists while not overspending. Retailers are meeting consumers where they are and encouraging them to spend by hosting sales online and in stores for multiple weeks, giving people the opportunity to shop when and where they want with plenty of time to browse deals and compare prices, says Steinman. What is the average savings on Black Friday? On average, Adobe expects to see discounts up to 30 percent off an item’s listed price during Cyber Week 2026, which is on par with 2025. That’s likely lower than what you think of when you hear “Black Friday deal,” but it is, for the most part, the new norm. Higher tariff fees and fuel prices, among other economic pressures, aren’t letting retailers discount items as aggressively as they have in years past and still make a profit. That doesn’t mean deals are “bad” — it more so means shoppers need to shift their mindset and look at the positives: that retailers are still participating in Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which ultimately benefits anyone looking to save. As for products discounted by 30 to 70 percent, they’re still out there, but they account for a much smaller portion of retailers’ offers compared to a few years ago. What are the most popular products to buy on Black Friday? The most popular products to buy on Black Friday are toys; tech; clothes and shoes; small home and kitchen appliances; subscriptions and experiences; and gift cards, according to experts. Deals tend to be the strongest in these categories, too — retailers know they’re common gifts, so they drop prices to make items extra enticing. That said, shoppers aren’t just using Black Friday to prepare for the holidays anymore. There’s been a recent surge in people buying products for themselves: planned spending on self-gifting increased 44 percent year over year, from $302 to $435, while spending on gifts for others has remained relatively steady, according to a recent survey from RetailMeNot. Economic instability is a strong contributing factor to this trend. People may have held off on crossing items off their personal wish lists throughout the year if their budgets got tighter, but Black Friday discounts makes shopping for themselves feel less like a splurge. Do products sell out on Black Friday? Yes, products sell out on Black Friday. Historically, more people shop on Black Friday than any other day of the year, so you’re competing with the biggest pool of consumers, many of whom are going after the same popular products. Toys and tech tend to sell out the fastest, as do clothes and shoes in specific sizes and colors. Shopping early benefits you here — the sooner you add to cart and check out, the more likely you are to get exactly what you want. There’s one more reason why products sell out: limited inventory. “Following the tariff disruptions, many retailers are maintaining leaner inventories to protect their margins, which leaves less excess stock to be cleared at deep discounts,” says Townsend. For shoppers, this means jumping on deals quickly is more important than ever — this is not the year to wait until Cyber Monday. Why is Black Friday called Black Friday? The term “Black Friday” originally had no connection to shopping, says Nancy Koehn, a historian and professor at the Harvard Business School. It described a financial panic in 1869 that resulted from investors Jay Gould and Jim Fisk driving up gold prices and ultimately causing the market to crash. Since its 19th-century inception, the term “Black Friday” has generally been used to describe other negative events, such as workers not showing up for work the day after Thanksgiving, says Koehn. The first time “Black Friday” specifically referred to shopping the day after Thanksgiving was in the 1950s. Police in Philadelphia complained about an influx of people coming to the city to shop the day after Thanksgiving, calling it a “Black Friday” because they had to control crowds. From there, the term came to describe shopping on that day and gained momentum each year. Originally, retailers were upset about the name “Black Friday” because the term had a negative connotation, says Koehn. There were efforts to call it “Big Friday” instead, but they ultimately failed. Retailers then changed the narrative and decided that Black Friday is when they’re supposed to be “in the black,” a financial term describing a business’s profitability and prosperity, in contrast to being “in the red,” or in a deficit. Koehn says the idea of positioning Black Friday as a shopping holiday “galloped forward” between the 1970s and 1980s, which she attributes to retailers instigating competition among themselves and expanding the deals they offered. Overall, “there was no defining moment that made us call Black Friday ‘Black Friday,’” says Koehn. “It’s really the evolution of language and definition, retail practices and consumers responding to that.” Meet our retail experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. I’ve written about the history of both events, and explained what to buy and what to skip during each one. I’ve also appeared in Black Friday and Cyber Monday-related NBC News NOW and TODAY broadcast segments. Additionally, I cover the best deals during all major shopping holidays throughout the year, and how economic instability is impacting shopping habits and prices on consumer goods. articles.title: ‘It’s always an option’: Trump open to pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang; urges him not to plead Fifth before Congress
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he is open to pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over potential crimes, but believes such a move will not be necessary.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has said he is open to pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over potential crimes, but believes such a move will not be necessary. Trump also urged the chipmaker's chief executive to tell the truth when he faces congressional questioning next week amid scrutiny over his alleged links to a woman suspected of having connections to Chinese intelligence.In an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, Trump was asked whether he would consider granting Huang a presidential pardon.“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” the president said.Trump also said he did not believe Huang needed to invoke his Fifth Amendment right, which allows individuals in the US to refuse to answer questions that could incriminate them, during his upcoming congressional testimony.“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said.“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person,” he added.According to CNN, Huang is scheduled to testify behind closed doors before a US Senate committee on Tuesday next week, followed by a public hearing with lawmakers on Friday. The questioning is expected to focus on US export controls and Nvidia's business dealings involving China.Why is Jensen Huang facing scrutiny?Huang's upcoming testimony comes amid questions surrounding his relationship with a Chinese woman suspected by US intelligence officials of having links to Chinese intelligence. The Nvidia chief has acknowledged having an affair with the woman.The controversy has also drawn attention to the company's compliance with US restrictions on exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China, particularly allegations that Nvidia chips may have been diverted to Chinese AI companies through third countries.The developments have prompted lawmakers to seek answers about the company's export practices and the potential national security implications of its business dealings.Trump's remarks came a day after Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as chief executive, following his removal from the position less than two weeks earlier. The president had taken credit for persuading the company's board to bring Huang back.The decision also triggered a sharp rally in Nvidia shares. The Guardian reported that the rise in the company's stock potentially increased the value of Trump's holdings by as much as $15 million in a single day.During his interview with the New York Post, Trump also referred to the stock's recovery, saying, "That's not bad, went down a couple of points," before adding, "it really picked up at the end."Meanwhile, the president defended Huang despite the controversy, saying he had always considered the Nvidia chief to be trustworthy and intelligent.You use AI every day.
